topics.title: Arrays, Stacks, Queues and Linked Lists
topics.summary: Address arithmetic, the cost table for linear structures, circular queues, and the stack algorithms for infix, postfix and prefix expressions.

blocks.text:
## Why linear structures differ at all

Every linear data structure stores a sequence. What separates them is not what they hold but **which operations are cheap**, and that follows entirely from how the elements are laid out in memory.

An **array** is one contiguous block. Because element $i$ sits at a position you can compute with multiplication and addition, reaching any element costs the same constant time. The price is that the block has a fixed size and that the elements are packed with no gaps, so making room in the middle means physically shifting everything after it.

A **linked list** stores each element in its own node together with the address of the next node. Nothing is contiguous, so nothing has to shift: splicing a node in or out is a couple of pointer writes. The price is that you can only reach element $i$ by walking from the head, and that every element carries the memory overhead of one or two pointers.

**Stacks** and **queues** are not new layouts at all. They are arrays or lists with the interface deliberately restricted — a stack to one end, a queue to one end for insertion and the other for removal. The restriction is the point: it makes both operations $O(1)$ and it makes the structure match a problem whose natural order is last-in-first-out or first-in-first-out.

Exam questions almost never ask you to define these. They ask for a cost, an address, a count, or the contents of the structure after a given sequence of operations.

## Array address arithmetic

For a one-dimensional array $A$ with lower bound $L$, base address $B$ and element size $w$ bytes:

$$\text{addr}(A[i]) = B + w\,(i - L)$$

For a two-dimensional array $A[L_1 \ldots U_1][L_2 \ldots U_2]$ write $n_1 = U_1 - L_1 + 1$ rows and $n_2 = U_2 - L_2 + 1$ columns. Then

$$\textbf{row-major: }\ \text{addr}(A[i][j]) = B + w\big[(i - L_1)\,n_2 + (j - L_2)\big]$$
$$\textbf{column-major: }\ \text{addr}(A[i][j]) = B + w\big[(j - L_2)\,n_1 + (i - L_1)\big]$$

The rule to remember without memorising two formulas: **the index that varies fastest in storage order is the one that is added last, and the other index is multiplied by the number of positions in the fast dimension.** Row-major (C, Java, Python) stores a whole row before starting the next, so columns vary fastest and you multiply the row offset by $n_2$. Column-major (FORTRAN, MATLAB) is the mirror image.

For three dimensions, row-major generalises by nesting:

$$\text{addr}(A[i][j][k]) = B + w\Big[\big((i-L_1)n_2 + (j-L_2)\big)n_3 + (k-L_3)\Big]$$

**Sparse matrices** are stored as a list of $(\text{row}, \text{col}, \text{value})$ triples. A matrix with $n$ non-zero entries in an $m \times p$ grid needs $3(n+1)$ integers in triple form against $mp$ in dense form, so triples win once $n < mp/3$. An **upper triangular** $n \times n$ matrix stored in a 1-D array of $n(n+1)/2$ cells puts $A[i][j]$ (1-based, $i \le j$) at offset $(i-1)n - \frac{(i-1)(i-2)}{2} + (j - i)$.

blocks.title: Worked example — row-major and column-major addresses
blocks.text:
An array `A[1..8][1..10]` of 4-byte integers has base address 2000. Find the address of `A[5][7]` under both storage orders.

Here $L_1 = L_2 = 1$, $n_1 = 8$ rows, $n_2 = 10$ columns, $w = 4$, $B = 2000$.

**Row-major.** Elements before `A[5][7]`: four complete rows ($4 \times 10 = 40$) plus six elements of row 5, so 46 elements.

$$\text{addr} = 2000 + 4\big[(5-1)\times 10 + (7-1)\big] = 2000 + 4(40 + 6) = 2000 + 184 = 2184$$

**Column-major.** Elements before it: six complete columns ($6 \times 8 = 48$) plus four elements of column 7, so 52 elements.

$$\text{addr} = 2000 + 4\big[(7-1)\times 8 + (5-1)\big] = 2000 + 4(48 + 4) = 2000 + 208 = 2208$$

Notice the two answers differ, and that the *only* structural difference is whether you multiply by 10 (the column count) or by 8 (the row count). If a question gives you both an answer and the base and asks for the dimension, solve the same equation for $n_2$ or $n_1$.

**Reverse direction.** Suppose the same array is row-major with 4-byte elements, `A[1][1]` is at 2000 and `A[4][6]` is found at 2140. Is that consistent with 10 columns? $(2140-2000)/4 = 35$ elements before it, and $(4-1)n_2 + (6-1) = 35$ gives $3n_2 = 30$, so $n_2 = 10$. Consistent.

## Linked lists and the cost table

| Operation | Array | Singly linked | Doubly linked |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access $i$-th element | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Search for a key (unsorted) | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Insert at front | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Insert at rear (tail pointer kept) | $O(1)$ amortised | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Insert after a given node | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Delete a node given a pointer **to it** | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ trick, $O(n)$ honestly | $O(1)$ |
| Delete the last node (tail pointer kept) | $O(1)$ | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ |
| Extra memory per element | 0 | 1 pointer | 2 pointers |

Two rows deserve comment.

**Deleting a node of a singly linked list given only a pointer to it.** You cannot unlink it directly because you cannot reach its predecessor. The standard trick is to copy the *successor's* data into the current node and unlink the successor instead, which is $O(1)$ — but it fails for the last node, and it invalidates any external pointer to the successor. In a doubly linked list the predecessor is available, so a genuine $O(1)$ deletion is possible for any node, which is exactly why deletion-heavy structures such as LRU caches use doubly linked lists.

**Circular lists.** A circular singly linked list with a pointer to the **last** node gives $O(1)$ access to both ends, because `last->next` is the head. Keeping a pointer to the first node instead makes rear insertion $O(n)$. That asymmetry is a favourite one-mark question.

A **header node** (a dummy first node holding no data) removes every special case for insertion and deletion at the front, at the cost of one extra node. A **circular doubly linked list with a header** has no `NULL` pointers at all.

**Josephus, reversal and cycle detection** are the three classic linked-list algorithm questions. Reversing a singly linked list iteratively needs exactly three pointers (`prev`, `curr`, `next`) and $O(n)$ time with $O(1)$ space. Cycle detection uses **Floyd's tortoise and hare**: a slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two meet inside the cycle if and only if a cycle exists, in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space; restarting the slow pointer at the head and advancing both one step at a time then meets at the cycle's entry node.

## Stacks

A stack supports `push`, `pop`, `top` and `isEmpty`, all $O(1)$. In an array implementation a single `top` index (initialised to $-1$) is all the state you need; overflow is `top == n-1` and underflow is `top == -1`.

**Two stacks in one array** should grow towards each other from opposite ends: stack 1 from index 0 upwards, stack 2 from index $n-1$ downwards, with overflow only when `top1 + 1 == top2`. This wastes nothing, whereas splitting the array in half can overflow while half the array is free.

The important uses:

- **Function calls.** Each call pushes an activation record; recursion depth is stack depth. A recursion of depth $d$ needs $\Theta(d)$ stack space, which is why the space complexity of quicksort is $O(\log n)$ on average but $O(n)$ in the worst case.
- **Expression handling** — conversion and evaluation, below.
- **Backtracking and iterative DFS.** Replacing a queue by a stack in a graph traversal turns BFS into (a variant of) DFS.
- **Balanced-parenthesis checking**, undo logs, and the browser back button.

**Implementing a queue with two stacks.** Push onto `in`. To dequeue, if `out` is empty pour all of `in` into `out`, then pop `out`. Each element is moved at most twice, so dequeue is $O(1)$ **amortised**, though a single dequeue can cost $O(n)$. **Implementing a stack with two queues** costs $O(n)$ on one of the two operations, whichever you choose to make expensive; there is no amortised escape.

## Queues and the circular queue formulas

A linear array queue with `front` and `rear` indices suffers from false overflow: after several enqueues and dequeues `rear` reaches the end while the front of the array is empty. The fix is the **circular queue**, in which both indices wrap with `(index + 1) % n`.

With the usual convention that `front` indexes the first element, `rear` indexes the last element, and both start at $-1$:

- **Empty**: `front == -1`
- **Full**: `(rear + 1) % n == front`
- **Number of elements**: $(\text{rear} - \text{front} + n) \bmod n + 1$ when non-empty

With the alternative convention that `rear` indexes the **next free slot** and both start at 0, one slot is deliberately left unused so that empty and full can be told apart:

- **Empty**: `front == rear`
- **Full**: `(rear + 1) % n == front`
- **Number of elements**: $(\text{rear} - \text{front} + n) \bmod n$
- **Usable capacity**: $n - 1$

Always check which convention the question uses; the phrase "one position is kept vacant" or a stated capacity of $n-1$ tells you it is the second.

**Deques** allow insertion and deletion at both ends; an **input-restricted deque** forbids insertion at one end, an **output-restricted deque** forbids deletion at one end. A **priority queue** ignores arrival order entirely and serves by key; the standard implementation is a binary heap giving $O(\log n)$ insert and extract, covered in topic 7.2.

## Expression notation and conversion

An infix expression needs precedence rules and parentheses to be unambiguous. **Postfix** (reverse Polish) and **prefix** (Polish) need neither — the operator order in the string fixes the evaluation order completely, which is why compilers and calculators convert to postfix before generating code.

Operator precedence, highest first: `^` (exponentiation, **right**-associative), then `*` `/` `%`, then `+` `-`, all left-associative.

**Infix to postfix (the shunting-yard procedure).** Scan the infix string left to right with one operator stack and one output string.

items: If the token is an operand, append it to the output immediately.
If it is ')', pop and output operators until '(' is popped; discard both parentheses.
If it is a left-associative operator, pop and output every stack operator whose precedence is greater than or equal to it (stopping at '('), then push it.
If it is the right-associative '^', pop only operators of strictly greater precedence, then push it.
At end of input, pop and output the rest of the stack.

blocks.text:
**Infix to prefix** is the same algorithm run in mirror image: reverse the infix string, swap every `(` with `)`, convert to postfix (with the associativity rules for `^` flipped), then reverse the result. Trying to convert directly left to right is where marks are lost.

**Evaluation.** A postfix string is evaluated left to right with one operand stack: push operands, and on each operator pop two operands — the **second one popped is the left operand** — apply, push the result. A prefix string is evaluated the same way but scanned **right to left**, and there the *first* popped value is the left operand. At the end the single stack entry is the answer.

**Maximum stack depth** during postfix evaluation equals the largest number of operands pending at any point, which is a common numerical question: simulate and record the peak.

blocks.title: Worked example — conversion and evaluation
blocks.text:
**(a) Convert $A + B \times (C \verb|^| D - E) \verb|^| (F + G \times H) - I$ to postfix.**

| Token | Stack after | Output after |
|---|---|---|
| `A` | | `A` |
| `+` | `+` | `A` |
| `B` | `+` | `A B` |
| `*` | `+ *` | `A B` |
| `(` | `+ * (` | `A B` |
| `C` | `+ * (` | `A B C` |
| `^` | `+ * ( ^` | `A B C` |
| `D` | `+ * ( ^` | `A B C D` |
| `-` | `+ * ( -` | `A B C D ^` |
| `E` | `+ * ( -` | `A B C D ^ E` |
| `)` | `+ *` | `A B C D ^ E -` |
| `^` | `+ * ^` | `A B C D ^ E -` |
| `(` | `+ * ^ (` | |
| `F` | `+ * ^ (` | `... F` |
| `+` | `+ * ^ ( +` | |
| `G` | `+ * ^ ( +` | `... F G` |
| `*` | `+ * ^ ( + *` | |
| `H` | `+ * ^ ( + *` | `... F G H` |
| `)` | `+ * ^` | `... F G H * +` |
| `-` | `-` | `... F G H * + ^ * +` |
| `I` | `-` | `... I` |
| end | | `A B C D ^ E - F G H * + ^ * + I -` |

At the `^` after `)` the stack top is `*`; since `^` outranks `*` nothing is popped. At the final `-` everything of precedence $\ge$ `-` comes off: `^`, then `*`, then `+`.

**Answer:** `ABCD^E-FGH*+^*+I-`

**(b) Evaluate the postfix expression `5 6 2 + * 12 4 / -`.**

| Token | Action | Stack |
|---|---|---|
| `5` | push | 5 |
| `6` | push | 5, 6 |
| `2` | push | 5, 6, 2 |
| `+` | $6+2=8$ | 5, 8 |
| `*` | $5 \times 8 = 40$ | 40 |
| `12` | push | 40, 12 |
| `4` | push | 40, 12, 4 |
| `/` | $12/4 = 3$ | 40, 3 |
| `-` | $40 - 3 = 37$ | 37 |

**Answer: 37.** The maximum stack depth reached is 3.

Note the subtraction: the top of the stack at that moment is 3 and below it is 40, and the result is $40 - 3$, not $3 - 40$. Getting this backwards on a non-commutative operator is the single most common arithmetic slip in this topic.

blocks.q: A circular queue is implemented in an array of size 10 with `front` pointing at the first element and `rear` at the last element. If `front = 7` and `rear = 2`, how many elements are in the queue?
blocks.exp: With this convention the count is $(\text{rear} - \text{front} + n) \bmod n + 1 = (2 - 7 + 10) \bmod 10 + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6$. Check by listing the occupied slots as the queue wraps: 7, 8, 9, 0, 1, 2 — six slots.

blocks.q: Which single change makes deletion of an arbitrary node, given only a pointer to that node, genuinely $O(1)$ in all cases?
opts: Adding a previous pointer to each node
blocks.exp: Deletion needs the predecessor. Only a `prev` pointer supplies it directly, which is the doubly linked list. A header node and a tail pointer help at the ends but not in the middle, and a circular singly linked list still forces an $O(n)$ walk to find the predecessor.

blocks.q: The prefix form of the infix expression $(A + B) \times (C - D)$ is
blocks.exp: In prefix the operator precedes its two operands. The top-level operator is `*`, applied to $(A+B)$ which is `+AB` and $(C-D)$ which is `-CD`, giving `*+AB-CD`. Option 3 is the postfix form; option 1 misplaces the top-level operator.

tricks.title: Count elements before, not indices
tricks.body: Every array-address question reduces to 'how many elements sit before this one'. Count that number $k$, then the address is $B + wk$. You never need to remember whether the formula uses $n_1$ or $n_2$ — row-major puts $n_2$ (the column count) as the multiplier because that is how many elements a complete row contains.

tricks.title: Postfix conversion: operand order never changes
tricks.body: In postfix and prefix, the operands appear in exactly the same left-to-right order as in the infix expression (prefix after the final reversal). If your answer scrambles the letters, it is wrong without further checking — eliminate those options immediately.

tricks.title: Infix to prefix = reverse, swap brackets, postfix, reverse
tricks.body: Never convert to prefix directly. Reverse the string, exchange every '(' and ')', run the ordinary postfix algorithm, reverse the output. Only the associativity of '^' needs flipping during the middle step.

tricks.title: Circular queue: the wasted slot tells you the convention
tricks.body: If a question says capacity is $n-1$ or 'one cell is always empty', use count $= (r-f+n) \bmod n$. If it says both pointers start at $-1$ and rear marks the last element, use $(r-f+n)\bmod n + 1$. Deciding this first saves an off-by-one.

tricks.title: Two stacks grow inward; two queues do not help
tricks.body: For two stacks in one array of size $n$, grow from both ends and overflow only when they meet — total capacity $n$. But building a stack from two queues cannot beat $O(n)$ on one operation, while a queue from two stacks is $O(1)$ amortised. The asymmetry is asked about directly.

traps.title: Amortised $O(1)$ is not worst-case $O(1)$
traps.body: The two-stack queue has $O(1)$ amortised dequeue, but a single dequeue that triggers the transfer costs $\Theta(n)$. A question asking for the *worst-case* cost of one dequeue wants $O(n)$; a question asking for the cost of $n$ dequeues wants $O(n)$ total, i.e. $O(1)$ each.

traps.title: The right-associativity of '^'
traps.body: $2 \verb|^| 3 \verb|^| 2$ is $2^{(3^2)} = 512$, not $(2^3)^2 = 64$. In conversion, an incoming '^' pops only operators of **strictly greater** precedence, so an existing '^' on the stack stays put. Every other operator pops equal precedence.

traps.title: Operand order when popping
traps.body: For `a b -` the value is $a - b$: the second element popped is the left operand. For prefix scanned right to left it is the opposite — the first popped is the left operand. Subtraction and division are where this costs marks; addition and multiplication hide the error.

traps.title: Access versus insertion in a linked list
traps.body: 'Insertion into a linked list is $O(1)$' is true only when you already hold a pointer to the insertion point. Inserting at position $k$ of a list is $\Theta(k)$ because you must walk there first. Several options in an exam deliberately offer $O(1)$ for this.

topics.title: Trees: Binary, BST, AVL, B and B+ Trees, Heaps
topics.summary: Counting formulas for binary trees, traversal reconstruction, AVL rotations and minimum-node counts, B/B+ tree order and height bounds, and heap operations.

blocks.text:
## Counting facts for binary trees

Fix the convention that the **root is at level 0** and that the **height of a single node is 0**; an empty tree has height $-1$. Almost every discrepancy between two textbooks on this topic is a disagreement about these two conventions, so state them before you compute.

- Maximum nodes at level $l$: $2^l$.
- Maximum nodes in a tree of height $h$: $2^{h+1} - 1$.
- Minimum height of a binary tree with $n$ nodes: $\lceil \log_2 (n+1) \rceil - 1$, equivalently $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$.
- Maximum height with $n$ nodes: $n - 1$ (a degenerate chain).

A **strict** (or full, or proper) binary tree has every node with 0 or 2 children. In such a tree, with $n_0$ leaves and $n_2$ internal nodes of degree 2:

$$n_0 = n_2 + 1$$

The proof is a one-line edge count: every node except the root has exactly one incoming edge, so $n - 1$ edges; every degree-2 node emits two, so $2n_2$ edges; hence $2n_2 = n_0 + n_2 - 1$. The same identity generalises to $m$-ary trees as $n_0 = (m-1)n_m + 1$.

A **complete** binary tree fills every level except possibly the last, which fills left to right; it has height $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ and $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ leaves. A **perfect** tree has all $2^{h+1}-1$ nodes.

**Number of distinct binary tree shapes on $n$ nodes** is the Catalan number

$$C_n = \frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n} = \frac{(2n)!}{n!\,(n+1)!}$$

giving $1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132$ for $n = 0 \ldots 6$. The number of distinct **BSTs** on $n$ given distinct keys is the same $C_n$, because the shape determines the BST uniquely. The number of **labelled** binary trees on $n$ nodes is $C_n \cdot n!$.

A binary tree with $n$ nodes has $2n$ child pointers of which $n-1$ are used, so it has $n+1$ **NULL** links. Threaded binary trees reuse exactly those $n+1$ links to point at inorder predecessors and successors.

## Traversals and reconstruction

- **Inorder** (L, root, R), **preorder** (root, L, R), **postorder** (L, R, root), plus **level order** using a queue.
- All are $\Theta(n)$ time; recursive versions use $O(h)$ stack space, which is $O(n)$ for a skewed tree.
- **Inorder of a BST is the sorted key sequence.** This one fact answers a startling number of questions.

Reconstruction rules, which examiners test constantly:

| Given | Unique tree? |
|---|---|
| inorder + preorder | **yes** |
| inorder + postorder | **yes** |
| inorder + level order | **yes** |
| preorder + postorder | **no** for general binary trees; **yes** for strict binary trees |
| preorder alone, of a **BST** | **yes** (the BST property supplies the inorder) |
| postorder alone, of a **BST** | **yes** |

The pattern is simple: **inorder is what splits a sequence into a left part and a right part.** Without it, or without an extra structural promise such as "every node has 0 or 2 children" or "it is a BST", you cannot tell a left child from a right child in a one-child node.

## Binary search trees

Search, insert and delete are all $O(h)$, which is $O(\log n)$ when balanced and $\Theta(n)$ for a tree built by inserting sorted keys. Deletion has three cases:

1. **Leaf** — remove it.
2. **One child** — splice the child into the node's place.
3. **Two children** — replace the key with its **inorder successor** (leftmost node of the right subtree) or **inorder predecessor** (rightmost node of the left subtree), then delete that node, which necessarily has at most one child.

Because either choice is legal in case 3, a question about "the tree after deleting $x$" must say which is used; if it does not, the successor is the default.

Average height of a BST built from $n$ keys inserted in random order is $\Theta(\log n)$ — precisely about $4.31 \log_2 n$ — but the worst case remains $n-1$. That gap is exactly what self-balancing trees remove.

## AVL trees

An **AVL tree** is a BST in which, for every node,

$$\text{balance factor} = \text{height(left)} - \text{height(right)} \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$$

After an insertion, walk back up to the first node whose balance factor becomes $\pm 2$ — the lowest such node — and rotate there. Name the case by the **two steps from that unbalanced node towards the newly inserted key**:

| Case | Shape | Fix | Rotations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LL** | left child's left subtree | single **right** rotation at the unbalanced node | 1 |
| **RR** | right child's right subtree | single **left** rotation | 1 |
| **LR** | left child's right subtree | left-rotate the child, then right-rotate the node | 2 |
| **RL** | right child's left subtree | right-rotate the child, then left-rotate the node | 2 |

**One rotation (single or double) always suffices after an insertion.** After a **deletion** that is no longer true: rebalancing can cascade all the way to the root, needing up to $O(\log n)$ rotations. That asymmetry is asked directly.

**Minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height $h$** satisfies

$$N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1, \qquad N(0) = 1,\ N(1) = 2$$

giving $1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88, 143, 232$ for $h = 0, 1, \ldots, 10$. These are the Fibonacci numbers shifted: $N(h) = F_{h+3} - 1$. Inverting the recurrence gives the height bound

$$h < 1.44 \log_2 (n + 2) - 0.328$$

so an AVL tree is at most about 44% taller than a perfectly balanced tree. A **red-black tree** is looser — height $\le 2\log_2(n+1)$ — so it does fewer rotations on update but more comparisons on search, which is the standard comparison question.

blocks.title: Worked example — AVL insertions with an RL rotation
blocks.text:
Insert 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 25 into an empty AVL tree.

**10, 20.** No violation. Tree: 10 with right child 20.

**30.** Node 10 now has balance factor $0 - 1 = $ height(left) $-$ height(right) $= -1 - 1 = -2$. The path from 10 to 30 goes right then right, so this is **RR**: single left rotation at 10.

Tree: root 20, left 10, right 30. All balance factors 0.

**40.** Goes right of 30. Balance factors: node 30 is $-1$, node 20 is $\text{height(10)} - \text{height(30 subtree)} = 0 - 1 = -1$. Legal, no rotation.

**50.** Goes right of 40. Now node 30 has balance factor $-2$, and the path 30 $\to$ 40 $\to$ 50 is right-right, so **RR**: left-rotate at 30. The subtree becomes 40 with children 30 and 50.

Tree: root 20; left child 10; right child 40 with children 30 and 50.

**25.** BST insertion: $25 > 20$ so go right to 40; $25 < 40$ go left to 30; $25 < 30$ go left — 25 becomes the left child of 30.

Now recompute heights bottom-up. Node 25: height 0. Node 30: left subtree height 0, right empty $(-1)$, balance $= +1$, legal, height 1. Node 50: height 0. Node 40: left subtree (30) height 1, right subtree (50) height 0, balance $= +1$, legal, height 2. Node 20: left subtree (10) height 0, right subtree (40) height 2, balance $= 0 - 2 = -2$ — **unbalanced at the root**.

The path from 20 towards 25 is right (to 40) then left (to 30): this is the **RL** case. Two rotations:

1. **Right-rotate at 40.** 30 rises; 40 becomes 30's right child; 25 stays as 30's left child; 50 stays as 40's right child. The right subtree of 20 is now 30 with children 25 and 40, and 40 has right child 50.
2. **Left-rotate at 20.** 30 becomes the root; 20 takes 30's left subtree (25) as its right child and keeps 10 as its left child; 40 remains 30's right child.

**Final tree:** root 30; left child 20 with children 10 and 25; right child 40 with right child 50.

Verify: inorder is 10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50 — sorted, so it is still a BST. Balance factors: 10, 25, 50 are leaves (0); 20 has two leaf children (0); 40 has left empty, right height 0, balance $-1$; 30 has left height 1, right height 1, balance 0. All within $\pm 1$.

## B-trees

A **B-tree of order $m$** is a balanced multiway search tree designed for disk: one node is one disk block, so a high branching factor makes the tree shallow and the number of disk reads small. The rules:

- Every node has at most $m$ children and at most $m-1$ keys.
- Every node except the root has at least $\lceil m/2 \rceil$ children, i.e. at least $\lceil m/2 \rceil - 1$ keys.
- The root has at least 2 children (at least 1 key) unless it is a leaf.
- All leaves are at the same depth. The tree grows **upwards**, by splitting the root.
- A node with $k$ children holds $k-1$ keys, and its keys separate the children's key ranges.

Writing $t = \lceil m/2 \rceil$ for the **minimum degree**, a B-tree with $n$ keys has height

$$h \le \log_t \frac{n+1}{2} \qquad \text{(maximum, nodes minimally filled)}$$
$$h \ge \lceil \log_m (n+1) \rceil - 1 \qquad \text{(minimum, nodes completely full)}$$

Insertion pushes a key into a leaf; if the leaf overflows ($m$ keys), split it at the median, promote the median to the parent, and repeat upward. Deletion may **borrow** from a sibling with a spare key (rotating through the parent) or **merge** with a sibling and pull the separator down; underflow can also propagate upward, and the height falls only when the root is emptied.

**B+ tree** differs in exactly three respects, and these three are what a question tests:

1. **All data records (or record pointers) live in the leaves.** Internal nodes hold only separator keys, which may be duplicated in the leaves.
2. **Leaves are chained in a linked list**, so a range query finds the start once and then walks sequentially — the reason every real database index is a B+ tree.
3. Because internal nodes carry no data, more keys fit per block, so the fan-out is higher and the tree is shorter for the same $n$.

A consequence often asked: in a B-tree a successful search can stop at an internal node, so search time varies; in a B+ tree **every** search descends to a leaf, so every search costs the same and equals the height.

blocks.title: Worked example — B-tree order, capacity and height
blocks.text:
**(a) Order from block geometry.** A disk block is 1024 bytes. Each key is 10 bytes, each record pointer 8 bytes, each block pointer 6 bytes. What is the order of a B+ tree index (internal node)?

An internal node with $m$ block pointers holds $m-1$ keys:

$$6m + 10(m-1) \le 1024 \;\Longrightarrow\; 16m \le 1034 \;\Longrightarrow\; m \le 64.6$$

So the **order is 64**. Each internal node holds up to 63 keys and 64 pointers.

A leaf node holds $k$ (key, record-pointer) pairs plus one chain pointer:

$$18k + 6 \le 1024 \;\Longrightarrow\; k \le 56.5 \;\Longrightarrow\; k = 56$$

Note how leaf and internal capacities differ in a B+ tree — computing both from the same formula is a standard error.

**(b) Height bounds.** A B-tree of order $m = 5$ stores $n = 1000$ keys. Here $t = \lceil 5/2 \rceil = 3$.

*Minimum height* (every node full, 4 keys and 5 children): the number of keys a tree of height $h$ can hold is
$$4\,(1 + 5 + 5^2 + \cdots + 5^h) = 4 \cdot \frac{5^{h+1}-1}{4} = 5^{h+1} - 1$$
For $h = 3$: $5^4 - 1 = 624 < 1000$. For $h = 4$: $5^5 - 1 = 3124 \ge 1000$. **Minimum height is 4.**

*Maximum height* (minimally filled: root 1 key and 2 children, every other node 2 keys and 3 children): level $i \ge 1$ has $2 \cdot 3^{i-1}$ nodes, so the total key count for height $h$ is
$$1 + \sum_{i=1}^{h} 2 \cdot 3^{i-1} \cdot 2 = 1 + 4\cdot\frac{3^h - 1}{2} = 2 \cdot 3^h - 1$$
For $h = 5$: $2 \cdot 243 - 1 = 485 \le 1000$, so height 5 is reachable. For $h = 6$: $2 \cdot 729 - 1 = 1457 > 1000$, so height 6 would need more than 1000 keys. **Maximum height is 5.**

Cross-check with the formula: $h \le \log_3 \frac{1001}{2} = \log_3 500.5 = 5.66$, so $h \le 5$. Agrees.

**(c) A split.** Insert into a full order-5 leaf holding keys 10, 20, 30, 40 the new key 25. Sorted: 10, 20, 25, 30, 40 — five keys, one too many. Split at the **median 25**: left leaf keeps 10, 20; right leaf keeps 30, 40; the key 25 moves up into the parent. Each new leaf has 2 keys, meeting the minimum of $\lceil 5/2 \rceil - 1 = 2$.

## Heaps

A **binary max-heap** is a complete binary tree in which every node is $\ge$ its children (min-heap: $\le$). Completeness lets it live in an array with no pointers. With **1-based** indexing:

$$\text{left}(i) = 2i, \quad \text{right}(i) = 2i+1, \quad \text{parent}(i) = \lfloor i/2 \rfloor$$

With **0-based** indexing the children are $2i+1$ and $2i+2$ and the parent is $\lfloor (i-1)/2 \rfloor$. Mixing the two is the commonest arithmetic error in heap questions, so write down which one you are using.

| Operation | Cost |
|---|---|
| find max (min) | $\Theta(1)$ |
| insert (place at end, sift **up**) | $O(\log n)$ |
| extract max (swap with last, shrink, sift **down**) | $O(\log n)$ |
| delete arbitrary element (position known) | $O(\log n)$ |
| increase/decrease key | $O(\log n)$ |
| **build heap from an unsorted array** | $\Theta(n)$ |
| heapsort | $\Theta(n \log n)$, in place, **not stable** |
| search for an arbitrary key | $\Theta(n)$ |

**Why build-heap is $\Theta(n)$ and not $\Theta(n\log n)$.** Sifting down from index $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ down to 1 costs at most the node's height, and there are at most $\lceil n/2^{k+1}\rceil$ nodes of height $k$, so the total is
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor} \Big\lceil \frac{n}{2^{k+1}} \Big\rceil O(k) \;=\; O\!\left(n \sum_{k\ge0} \frac{k}{2^k}\right) = O(2n) = O(n)$$
because $\sum k/2^k = 2$. Inserting $n$ elements one at a time instead costs $\Theta(n \log n)$ — the two build methods have genuinely different complexities, and questions exploit that.

Other facts worth having ready: a heap on $n$ nodes has $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ leaves, and the leaves occupy array positions $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$ through $n$ (1-based). The second-largest element of a max-heap is a child of the root, so it is found in one comparison; the **third** largest is among only three candidates. The minimum of a max-heap is some leaf, so finding it takes $\Theta(n)$ inspections of $\lceil n/2\rceil$ leaves.

Related structures for the record: a **binomial heap** merges in $O(\log n)$; a **Fibonacci heap** gives $O(1)$ amortised insert and decrease-key with $O(\log n)$ amortised extract-min, which is what makes Dijkstra run in $O(E + V\log V)$.

blocks.title: Worked example — build a max-heap, then one extraction
blocks.text:
**Build a max-heap from $A = [4, 10, 3, 5, 1]$** using 1-based indexing.

`BUILD-HEAP` sifts down from $i = \lfloor 5/2 \rfloor = 2$ to $i = 1$.

*$i = 2$:* $A[2] = 10$, children $A[4] = 5$ and $A[5] = 1$. The largest of $\{10, 5, 1\}$ is already the parent, so nothing moves.

*$i = 1$:* $A[1] = 4$, children $A[2] = 10$ and $A[3] = 3$. Largest is 10 at index 2, so swap:
$$A = [10, 4, 3, 5, 1]$$
Continue sifting the 4 down from index 2: children $A[4] = 5$, $A[5] = 1$. Largest is 5 at index 4, so swap:
$$A = [10, 5, 3, 4, 1]$$
Index 4 is a leaf, so stop.

**Max-heap: $[10, 5, 3, 4, 1]$.** Check the property at every internal node: $10 \ge 5, 3$; $5 \ge 4, 1$. Valid.

**Now extract the maximum.** Swap $A[1]$ and $A[5]$, shrink to size 4: $[1, 5, 3, 4]$ with 10 removed. Sift 1 down from index 1: children $A[2]=5$, $A[3]=3$; largest is 5, swap $\to [5, 1, 3, 4]$. Continue at index 2: its only child is $A[4] = 4 > 1$, swap $\to [5, 4, 3, 1]$. Index 4 is a leaf.

**Heap after extraction: $[5, 4, 3, 1]$**, and the extracted value 10 now sits in the freed array slot — which is precisely how heapsort produces sorted output in place, one extraction at a time.

blocks.q: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 5 (a single node having height 0)?
blocks.exp: $N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1$ with $N(0)=1$, $N(1)=2$ gives $N(2)=4$, $N(3)=7$, $N(4)=12$, $N(5)=20$. Build the short table rather than recalling one value; the sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54 is worth knowing outright.

blocks.q: A B-tree of order 8 contains 1 key in its root and is 3 levels deep (height 2). What is the minimum possible number of keys in the whole tree?
blocks.exp: Minimum degree $t = \lceil 8/2 \rceil = 4$, so every non-root node holds at least $t-1 = 3$ keys and has at least $t = 4$ children, while the root may hold just 1 key and 2 children. Level 0: 1 key, 2 children. Level 1: 2 nodes carrying $2 \times 3 = 6$ keys and $2 \times 4 = 8$ children. Level 2: 8 leaves carrying $8 \times 3 = 24$ keys. Total $= 1 + 6 + 24 = 31$.

blocks.q: The postorder traversal of a binary search tree is 8, 12, 10, 16, 25, 20, 15. What is its preorder traversal?
blocks.exp: Postorder ends with the root, 15. Inorder of a BST is the sorted order 8, 10, 12, 15, 16, 20, 25, so the left subtree holds 8, 10, 12 and the right holds 16, 20, 25. Within the left part, postorder 8, 12, 10 makes 10 the root with children 8 and 12; within the right, 16, 25, 20 makes 20 the root with children 16 and 25. Preorder (root, left, right) is therefore 15, 10, 8, 12, 20, 16, 25.

tricks.title: Sort the keys to get the inorder for free
tricks.body: Any question about a BST that gives you one traversal has secretly given you two: the sorted key list is the inorder. Preorder + sorted, or postorder + sorted, reconstructs the tree uniquely — you never need to simulate insertions.

tricks.title: Name the AVL case by the two steps down to the new key
tricks.body: From the lowest unbalanced node, write the two directions you travel towards the inserted key: LL, RR, LR or RL. Same letters means one rotation in the opposite direction; different letters means two rotations. No need to reason about which subtree got taller.

tricks.title: AVL minimum-node sequence 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54
tricks.body: Memorise eight terms of $N(h)$. Questions of the form 'maximum height of an AVL tree with $n$ nodes' are answered by finding the largest $h$ with $N(h) \le n$, which takes one scan of this list.

tricks.title: B-tree minimum fill: root is the exception, everyone else has $\lceil m/2\rceil - 1$ keys
tricks.body: For maximum-height or minimum-key-count questions, fill the root with 1 key and 2 children and every other node with the bare minimum. For minimum-height or maximum-capacity questions, fill everything with $m-1$ keys and $m$ children. Both are geometric series you can sum in one line.

tricks.title: Leaves of a heap start at index $\lfloor n/2\rfloor + 1$
tricks.body: Build-heap loops from $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ down to 1 exactly because everything after that is already a valid one-node heap. This also answers 'how many leaves' ($\lceil n/2\rceil$) and 'where is the smallest element of a max-heap' (somewhere in that leaf range).

traps.title: Order of a B-tree: children, not keys
traps.body: Order $m$ means at most $m$ **children** and at most $m-1$ keys. A few older texts define order as the maximum number of keys. If a question says 'order 5' and the options fit only the 5-children reading, use it — but check the minimum, $\lceil m/2\rceil$ children, against the options to confirm which convention is in play.

traps.title: One rotation after insert, many after delete
traps.body: AVL insertion needs at most one single or double rotation. AVL **deletion** can require rebalancing at every node on the path to the root, up to $O(\log n)$ rotations. Any option claiming deletion also needs at most one rotation is wrong.

traps.title: Building a heap by repeated insertion is not $\Theta(n)$
traps.body: $n$ successive inserts cost $\Theta(n \log n)$; the bottom-up `BUILD-HEAP` costs $\Theta(n)$. The question usually says 'construct a heap from a given array', which means the linear method, but read the wording — 'insert the elements one by one' means the other one.

traps.title: Preorder plus postorder does not determine a tree
traps.body: They do determine a **strict** binary tree (every node 0 or 2 children) and a **BST** is determined by either one alone, but for a general binary tree a node with a single child cannot be placed. Inorder is the traversal that separates left from right.

topics.title: Hashing and Data Structures for Sets
topics.summary: Hash functions, chaining and every open-addressing scheme, load factor and expected probe counts, rehashing, Bloom filters and disjoint-set union-find.

blocks.text:
## What hashing buys and what it costs

A balanced search tree gives $O(\log n)$ lookup and keeps the keys in order. Hashing gives **expected $O(1)$** lookup and gives up order entirely: after hashing, "the next key after $k$" and "all keys in $[a,b]$" are no longer cheap. That trade is the whole design decision, and it is why database indexes are B+ trees (range queries) while symbol tables and language dictionaries are hash tables (point queries).

A hash table is an array of $m$ **slots** and a **hash function** $h$ mapping the universe of keys into $\{0, 1, \ldots, m-1\}$. Since the universe is far larger than $m$, two keys must sometimes collide. All of hashing is (a) choosing $h$ so collisions are rare and evenly spread, and (b) deciding what to do when one happens anyway.

The **load factor** is

$$\alpha = \frac{n}{m} = \frac{\text{number of keys stored}}{\text{number of slots}}$$

Every performance formula in this topic is a function of $\alpha$ alone, not of $n$ or $m$ separately. Under chaining $\alpha$ may exceed 1; under open addressing it cannot exceed 1, and performance degrades violently as it approaches 1.

## Hash functions

**Division method.** $h(k) = k \bmod m$. Fast, and good provided $m$ is chosen well: take $m$ **prime** and not close to a power of 2. If $m = 2^p$ then $h(k)$ is just the low $p$ bits of $k$, so any regularity in those bits (for instance all keys even) wrecks the distribution. If $m = 2^p - 1$ and keys are strings interpreted in radix $2^p$, permutations of a string hash identically.

**Multiplication method.** $h(k) = \lfloor m\,(kA \bmod 1) \rfloor$ for a constant $0 < A < 1$; here the value of $m$ does not matter, so $m = 2^p$ is convenient. Knuth's suggestion $A = (\sqrt5 - 1)/2 \approx 0.6180$ spreads well.

**Mid-square.** Square the key, take the middle digits. **Folding.** Split the key into equal-width pieces and add them. Both are older schemes still asked about by name.

**Universal hashing.** Pick $h$ at random at run time from a family $\mathcal H$ such that for any two distinct keys $x \ne y$, $\Pr_{h \in \mathcal H}[h(x) = h(y)] \le 1/m$. This makes the expected performance independent of the input, so no adversary and no unlucky data set can force worst-case behaviour. The standard family is $h_{a,b}(k) = ((ak + b) \bmod p) \bmod m$ with $p$ a prime larger than every key, $a \in \{1,\ldots,p-1\}$, $b \in \{0,\ldots,p-1\}$.

A hash function must be **deterministic**, must use the **whole** key, and should be cheap. It is not required to be, and cannot be, injective.

## Collision resolution

### Separate chaining
Each slot holds a linked list (or a small tree) of the keys that hash there.

- Insertion at the head is $\Theta(1)$ if duplicates need no check.
- Expected probes for an **unsuccessful** search: $\Theta(1 + \alpha)$ — you scan an average chain of length $\alpha$.
- Expected probes for a **successful** search: $\Theta(1 + \alpha/2)$ — on average you reach the middle of a chain.
- Worst case: all $n$ keys in one chain, $\Theta(n)$.
- $\alpha$ may exceed 1; deletion is trivial; extra memory is needed for pointers.

### Open addressing
All keys live in the array itself; a collision sends the key to another slot along a **probe sequence** $h(k,0), h(k,1), \ldots$ which should be a permutation of all $m$ slots.

**Linear probing:** $h(k,i) = (h'(k) + i) \bmod m$. Simplest, best cache behaviour, but suffers **primary clustering** — long runs of occupied slots form and grow, and any key hashing anywhere into a run must traverse the whole tail of it. Only $m$ distinct probe sequences exist.

**Quadratic probing:** $h(k,i) = (h'(k) + c_1 i + c_2 i^2) \bmod m$. Breaks up the runs, but two keys with the same initial slot follow the **same** sequence — **secondary clustering**. Also only $m$ distinct sequences. With $c_1 = c_2 = \tfrac12$ and $m$ a power of 2, the sequence hits every slot; with $h(k,i) = (h'(k) + i^2) \bmod m$ and $m$ prime, it is guaranteed to find a free slot only while the table is less than **half full**.

**Double hashing:** $h(k,i) = (h_1(k) + i\,h_2(k)) \bmod m$. Here $h_2(k)$ must be **relatively prime to $m$** for the sequence to cover the table — take $m$ prime and $h_2(k) \in \{1,\ldots,m-1\}$, or $m = 2^p$ and $h_2$ always odd. This gives $\Theta(m^2)$ distinct probe sequences and is the closest practical approximation to uniform hashing, so it clusters least.

### Expected probes
Under the idealisation of **uniform hashing**, with $\alpha < 1$:

$$\text{unsuccessful search} \le \frac{1}{1-\alpha}, \qquad \text{successful search} \le \frac{1}{\alpha}\ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$$

For **linear probing** specifically the constants are worse:

$$\text{unsuccessful} \approx \frac12\left(1 + \frac{1}{(1-\alpha)^2}\right), \qquad \text{successful} \approx \frac12\left(1 + \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\right)$$

An insertion costs the same as an unsuccessful search, because that is exactly what it performs first.

### Deletion under open addressing
You cannot simply empty a slot: that would break every probe sequence that passes through it, and later searches would stop early and wrongly report "absent". Mark the slot **deleted** (a tombstone) instead — searches probe past it, insertions may reuse it. Tombstones accumulate and eventually force a rebuild, which is one reason chaining is preferred when deletions are frequent.

### Rehashing
When $\alpha$ crosses a threshold (0.75 for Java's `HashMap`, 0.5 for many open-addressed tables), allocate a table of roughly double the size and **re-insert every key** — you cannot copy slots across, because $h$ depends on $m$. A single rehash costs $\Theta(n)$, but because the table size doubles each time the **amortised** cost per insertion stays $O(1)$.

blocks.title: Worked example — three probing schemes on the same keys
blocks.text:
Insert 12, 44, 13, 88, 23, 94, 11, 39, 20 into a table of size $m = 11$ with $h'(k) = k \bmod 11$.

Initial slots: $12 \to 1$, $44 \to 0$, $13 \to 2$, $88 \to 0$, $23 \to 1$, $94 \to 6$, $11 \to 0$, $39 \to 6$, $20 \to 9$.

**Linear probing**, $h(k,i) = (h'(k) + i) \bmod 11$:

| Key | Home | Probes | Lands at |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12 | 1 | — | 1 |
| 44 | 0 | — | 0 |
| 13 | 2 | — | 2 |
| 88 | 0 | 0,1,2 busy | **3** |
| 23 | 1 | 1,2,3 busy | **4** |
| 94 | 6 | — | 6 |
| 11 | 0 | 0,1,2,3,4 busy | **5** |
| 39 | 6 | 6 busy | **7** |
| 20 | 9 | — | 9 |

Final table: `0:44  1:12  2:13  3:88  4:23  5:11  6:94  7:39  8:–  9:20  10:–`, $\alpha = 9/11 \approx 0.82$. Key 11 needed **6** probes — the primary cluster in slots 0–5 did that.

**Quadratic probing**, $h(k,i) = (h'(k) + i^2) \bmod 11$:

- 44 $\to$ 0; 12 $\to$ 1; 13 $\to$ 2.
- 88: $0$ busy, $0+1=1$ busy, $0+4=4$ free $\to$ **4**.
- 23: $1$ busy, $1+1 = 2$ busy, $1+4 = 5$ free $\to$ **5**.
- 94 $\to$ 6.
- 11: $0,1,4$ busy, $0+9 = 9$ free $\to$ **9**.
- 39: $6$ busy, $6+1 = 7$ free $\to$ **7**.
- 20: $9$ busy, $9+1 = 10$ free $\to$ **10**.

Final table: `0:44  1:12  2:13  3:–  4:88  5:23  6:94  7:39  8:–  9:11  10:20`. Key 11 needed 4 probes instead of 6, but notice that 88 and 23 and 11 all started at slot 0 or 1 and still shadowed each other — that is secondary clustering.

**Double hashing** with $h_2(k) = 7 - (k \bmod 7)$, which is always in $\{1,\ldots,7\}$ and coprime to the prime 11:

- 44 $\to$ 0; 12 $\to$ 1; 13 $\to$ 2.
- 88: home 0 busy. $h_2(88) = 7 - (88 \bmod 7) = 7 - 4 = 3$. Probe $0+3 = 3$, free $\to$ **3**.
- 23: home 1 busy. $h_2(23) = 7 - 2 = 5$. Probe $1+5 = 6$, free $\to$ **6**.
- 94: home $6$ now busy. $h_2(94) = 7 - (94 \bmod 7) = 7 - 3 = 4$. Probe $6+4 = 10$, free $\to$ **10**.
- 11: home 0 busy. $h_2(11) = 7 - 4 = 3$. Probes $3$ busy, $6$ busy, $9$ free $\to$ **9**.
- 39: home 6 busy. $h_2(39) = 7 - 4 = 3$. Probe $9$ busy, $12 \bmod 11 = 1$ busy, $4$ free $\to$ **4**.
- 20: home 9 busy. $h_2(20) = 7 - 6 = 1$. Probe $10$ busy, $0$ busy, $1$ busy, $2$ busy, $3$ busy, $4$ busy, $5$ free $\to$ **5**.

Final table: `0:44  1:12  2:13  3:88  4:39  5:20  6:23  7:–  8:–  9:11  10:94`. Keys that shared a home slot took different routes — the point of double hashing.

**Load-factor check.** At $\alpha = 9/11 = 0.818$ the uniform-hashing estimate for an unsuccessful search is $1/(1-0.818) = 5.5$ probes, and the linear-probing estimate is $\tfrac12(1 + 1/0.182^2) = \tfrac12(1 + 30.2) = 15.6$. The measured cost of inserting key 11 into the linear table, 6 probes, sits between the two — real tables this small are noisy, but the direction of the prediction is right, and it shows why $\alpha$ is kept well below 1.

## Perfect hashing, Bloom filters and other set structures

**Perfect hashing** applies when the key set is static and known in advance: a two-level scheme hashes into $m = n$ buckets and gives bucket $j$ with $n_j$ keys its own secondary table of size $n_j^2$, chosen from a universal family so it has no collisions. Expected total space is $\Theta(n)$ and **worst-case** lookup is $O(1)$ — the only scheme in this topic with a worst-case guarantee.

**Cuckoo hashing** keeps two tables and two hash functions; a key lives in one of exactly two slots, so lookup is $O(1)$ **worst case**, at the cost of insertions that may cascade and occasionally force a rehash.

**Bloom filters** answer set membership with no false negatives and a controlled false-positive rate, using $m$ bits and $k$ independent hash functions and storing no keys at all. Insert sets $k$ bits; a query reports "present" only if all $k$ bits are set. With $n$ keys inserted the false-positive probability is approximately

$$p \approx \left(1 - e^{-kn/m}\right)^{k}, \qquad \text{minimised at } k = \frac{m}{n}\ln 2$$

giving $p \approx 0.6185^{\,m/n}$. Elements cannot be deleted from a plain Bloom filter, because clearing a bit might unset it for another key.

**Disjoint sets (union-find)** maintain a partition under two operations: `FIND(x)`, returning a representative of $x$'s set, and `UNION(x,y)`, merging two sets. The standard forest implementation applies two heuristics:

- **Union by rank (or size):** attach the shorter tree under the taller one, keeping height $O(\log n)$ on its own.
- **Path compression:** during `FIND`, re-point every node on the path directly at the root.

With both, a sequence of $m$ operations on $n$ elements costs $O(m\,\alpha(n))$, where $\alpha$ is the inverse Ackermann function — below 5 for every $n$ that fits in the universe, so this is constant for practical purposes. With union by rank alone it is $O(m \log n)$; with path compression alone, $O(m \log n)$ amortised. Union-find is what makes Kruskal's algorithm run in $O(E \log E)$, and it is also the standard tool for connected components under incremental edge insertion and for cycle detection in an undirected graph.

blocks.q: A hash table of size 10 uses open addressing with $h(k,i) = (k \bmod 10 + i) \bmod 10$. The keys 43, 165, 62, 123, 142 are inserted in that order. Which slot holds 142?
blocks.exp: Home slots: $43 \to 3$, $165 \to 5$, $62 \to 2$. Then $123 \to 3$ is occupied, so it probes 4 and lands there. Now slots 2, 3, 4, 5 form one cluster, so $142 \to 2$ probes 2, 3, 4, 5 (all busy) and settles in slot **6** on its fifth probe. Counting the run length from the home slot is faster than re-deriving each probe.

blocks.q: In a hash table with $m = 1000$ slots holding $n = 700$ keys with separate chaining, the expected number of key comparisons in an unsuccessful search is closest to
blocks.exp: An unsuccessful search must walk one entire chain, whose expected length is $\alpha = 700/1000 = 0.7$, so 0.7 key comparisons on top of the $\Theta(1)$ hash computation. The $\Theta(1+\alpha)$ form counts that constant work as well; when the question says 'key comparisons' the answer is $\alpha$ itself.

blocks.q: For double hashing $h(k,i) = (h_1(k) + i\,h_2(k)) \bmod m$ to probe every slot of the table, what must hold?
opts: $m$ must be a power of two
blocks.exp: Repeatedly adding $d = h_2(k)$ modulo $m$ visits the whole table exactly when $\gcd(d,m) = 1$; otherwise it cycles through only $m/\gcd(d,m)$ slots. Two easy ways to guarantee it: make $m$ prime and $h_2(k) < m$ nonzero, or make $m$ a power of two and $h_2(k)$ always odd.

tricks.title: Every probe formula is a function of $\alpha$ only
tricks.body: Remember $1/(1-\alpha)$ for an unsuccessful uniform-hashing search and $\frac1\alpha \ln\frac{1}{1-\alpha}$ for a successful one; for chaining remember $\alpha$ and $\alpha/2$. Then any question reduces to computing $n/m$ and substituting. At $\alpha = 0.5$ the numbers are 2 and 1.39; at $\alpha = 0.9$ they are 10 and 2.56.

tricks.title: Insertion costs exactly what an unsuccessful search costs
tricks.body: An insert probes until it finds an empty slot, which is the definition of an unsuccessful search. Questions that ask for the cost of inserting the $(n{+}1)$-th key want $1/(1-\alpha)$ with $\alpha = n/m$.

tricks.title: Read the probe count off the cluster, not the formula
tricks.body: In a linear-probing trace, the number of probes for a key equals 1 plus the number of consecutive occupied slots from its home slot onwards. Draw the table once and read the run lengths; do not re-simulate each key.

tricks.title: Quadratic probing with $m$ prime only guarantees a slot while $\alpha < 1/2$
tricks.body: If a question shows a quadratic-probing insert failing in a table that still has free slots, this is why — $i^2 \bmod m$ visits only about half the slots. It is the standard 'surprising' answer.

tricks.title: Union-find: path compression flattens, union by rank shortens
tricks.body: Asked for the effect of one heuristic alone, the answer is $O(\log n)$ amortised for either; asked for both together, the answer is $O(\alpha(n))$, effectively constant. Never say $O(1)$ worst case for a single find.

traps.title: Deleting by emptying a slot breaks open addressing
traps.body: Any key whose probe sequence passed through the emptied slot becomes unfindable. The correct answer is a tombstone (a DELETED marker), not 'set the slot to NULL'. This is the classic 'which of the following is a disadvantage of open addressing' item.

traps.title: Load factor cannot exceed 1 under open addressing
traps.body: With chaining $\alpha$ may be 5 or 50. With any open-addressing scheme every key occupies a slot, so $n \le m$ and $\alpha \le 1$. An option offering $\alpha = 1.5$ for linear probing is a giveaway distractor.

traps.title: Primary versus secondary clustering
traps.body: Primary clustering is linear probing: keys with *different* home slots pile into one run. Secondary clustering is quadratic probing: keys with the *same* home slot follow identical sequences. Double hashing has neither. The words are almost always swapped in at least one option.

traps.title: A good hash function is not a collision-free one
traps.body: Collisions are unavoidable whenever the universe is bigger than the table, by pigeonhole. 'Minimises collisions and distributes keys uniformly' is the correct description; 'avoids collisions entirely' is only possible for a known static key set via perfect hashing.

topics.title: Sorting and Searching
topics.summary: Every sorting algorithm with its best, average and worst behaviour, stability and space; the comparison lower bound; counting sort and radix sort; binary and interpolation search.

blocks.text:
## The three properties that classify a sort

Beyond running time, every sorting algorithm is described by three properties that questions test far more often than the code.

**Stability.** A sort is stable if two records with equal keys keep their original relative order. This matters whenever you sort by one field after already sorting by another — sort by name, then stably by department, and within each department the names stay alphabetical. Merge sort, insertion sort, bubble sort, counting sort and radix sort are stable. Quicksort, heapsort, selection sort and shell sort are not, in their standard forms. Any sort can be *made* stable by appending the original index to the key, at the cost of $O(n)$ extra space.

**In-place.** A sort is in place if it uses $O(1)$ — or in the looser reading, $O(\log n)$ — auxiliary space beyond the input array. Merge sort on arrays is the famous non-in-place comparison sort, needing $\Theta(n)$ scratch space; on **linked lists** it is in place, which is why it is the sort of choice for lists.

**Adaptivity.** An adaptive sort runs faster on nearly sorted input. Insertion sort is the outstanding example: its running time is $\Theta(n + I)$ where $I$ is the number of inversions, so an array with $O(n)$ inversions is sorted in linear time.

An **inversion** is a pair $(i,j)$ with $i < j$ and $A[i] > A[j]$. A sorted array has 0 inversions; a reverse-sorted array has $\binom{n}{2} = n(n-1)/2$; a random permutation has $n(n-1)/4$ on average. Bubble sort and insertion sort each perform exactly one element exchange (or shift) per inversion, which is the cleanest way to count their swaps.

## The complexity table

| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Auxiliary space | Stable | In place |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble sort (with early-exit flag) | $\Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $O(1)$ | yes | yes |
| Selection sort | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $O(1)$ | no | yes |
| Insertion sort | $\Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $O(1)$ | yes | yes |
| Shell sort | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | depends on gaps | $\Theta(n^2)$ (Shell's gaps) | $O(1)$ | no | yes |
| Merge sort | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n)$ | yes | no |
| Quicksort | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $O(\log n)$ avg, $O(n)$ worst | no | yes |
| Heapsort | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $O(1)$ | no | yes |
| Counting sort | $\Theta(n+k)$ | $\Theta(n+k)$ | $\Theta(n+k)$ | $\Theta(n+k)$ | yes | no |
| Radix sort ($d$ passes, base $k$) | $\Theta(d(n+k))$ | $\Theta(d(n+k))$ | $\Theta(d(n+k))$ | $\Theta(n+k)$ | yes | no |
| Bucket sort (uniform input) | $\Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n)$ | yes | no |
| Tree sort (BST) | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n)$ | yes | no |

Notes on the rows that trip people up.

**Selection sort has no best case.** It scans the entire unsorted suffix for the minimum whether or not the array is already sorted, so it always performs exactly $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons. It does, however, perform only $n-1$ swaps — the fewest of any comparison sort, which is why it is used when writes are far more expensive than reads.

**Bubble sort's $\Theta(n)$ best case requires the early-exit flag.** Without it, the plain double loop always makes $n(n-1)/2$ comparisons.

**Heapsort's best case** on $n$ *distinct* elements is still $\Theta(n\log n)$; it becomes $\Theta(n)$ only when all elements are equal.

**Quicksort's worst case** is an already sorted (or reverse sorted) array when the pivot is the first or last element — the partition splits $n-1$ and $0$ every time, giving $T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n^2)$. Randomised pivot choice or median-of-three makes this vanishingly unlikely. Despite the worse worst case, quicksort beats merge sort in practice because its inner loop is tight and it is cache friendly.

**Quicksort's recursion depth** is $O(\log n)$ only if you recurse on the smaller partition and loop on the larger; the naive version has $O(n)$ stack depth in the worst case.

## Partitioning schemes and comparison counts

**Lomuto partition** takes the last element as pivot, keeps a boundary index $i$, and swaps every element $\le$ pivot to the front. It performs $n-1$ comparisons and places the pivot at its final position.

**Hoare partition** runs two indices inwards from both ends and swaps out-of-place pairs. It does about three times fewer swaps than Lomuto and handles equal keys better, but it does **not** put the pivot at its final position — it only returns a split point. A question asking "where is the pivot after partitioning" has different answers for the two schemes.

Useful exact counts:

- **Merge** of two sorted runs of length $p$ and $q$: at most $p + q - 1$ comparisons, at least $\min(p,q)$.
- **Merge sort** on $n = 2^k$ elements: at most $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ comparisons. For $n = 8$ that is $24 - 8 + 1 = 17$.
- **Comparison-sort lower bound.** A comparison sort is a decision tree with $n!$ leaves and therefore height at least $\lceil \log_2 (n!) \rceil = \Omega(n\log n)$ by Stirling. So no comparison sort can beat $\Theta(n\log n)$ in the worst case, and merge sort and heapsort are asymptotically optimal.
- **Minimum comparisons to find both the maximum and the minimum:** $\lceil 3n/2 \rceil - 2$, by comparing elements in pairs first.
- **Minimum comparisons to find the second largest:** $n + \lceil \log_2 n\rceil - 2$, using a tournament.
- **Minimum comparisons to find the maximum alone:** exactly $n-1$.

Counting sort, radix sort and bucket sort dodge the $\Omega(n\log n)$ bound because they are not comparison sorts: they use the *values* of keys as array indices. Counting sort is only sensible when the key range $k$ is $O(n)$; if $k = n^2$ it degrades to $\Theta(n^2)$. Radix sort applies counting sort digit by digit, **least significant digit first**, and it is correct only because counting sort is stable — an MSD-first version with an unstable inner sort produces garbage.

blocks.title: Worked example — one Lomuto partition and one radix sort
blocks.text:
**(a) Partition $A = [7, 2, 1, 6, 8, 5, 3, 4]$ (0-indexed) with Lomuto, pivot = last element = 4.**

Set $i = -1$ and scan $j = 0 \ldots 6$, swapping $A[j]$ forward whenever $A[j] \le 4$.

| $j$ | $A[j]$ | $\le 4$? | Action | Array |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 7 | no | — | 7 2 1 6 8 5 3 4 |
| 1 | 2 | yes | $i{=}0$, swap $A[0],A[1]$ | **2** 7 1 6 8 5 3 4 |
| 2 | 1 | yes | $i{=}1$, swap $A[1],A[2]$ | 2 **1** 7 6 8 5 3 4 |
| 3 | 6 | no | — | 2 1 7 6 8 5 3 4 |
| 4 | 8 | no | — | 2 1 7 6 8 5 3 4 |
| 5 | 5 | no | — | 2 1 7 6 8 5 3 4 |
| 6 | 3 | yes | $i{=}2$, swap $A[2],A[6]$ | 2 1 **3** 6 8 5 7 4 |

Finally swap $A[i+1] = A[3]$ with the pivot $A[7]$:

$$A = [2, 1, 3, \mathbf{4}, 8, 5, 7, 6]$$

The pivot 4 is at index 3, which is its final sorted position. Everything left of it is $\le 4$, everything right is $> 4$. Comparisons performed: 7, i.e. $n-1$. Quicksort now recurses on $[2,1,3]$ and $[8,5,7,6]$ — a 3/4 split, so this pivot was a good one.

**(b) LSD radix sort of $[329, 457, 657, 839, 436, 720, 355]$.**

*Pass 1, units digit:* keys ordered by last digit, ties keeping their previous order — 720 (0), 355 (5), 436 (6), 457 (7), 657 (7), 329 (9), 839 (9):
$$[720,\ 355,\ 436,\ 457,\ 657,\ 329,\ 839]$$

*Pass 2, tens digit:* digits are 720$\to$2, 355$\to$5, 436$\to$3, 457$\to$5, 657$\to$5, 329$\to$2, 839$\to$3. Stable ordering by that digit gives 720, 329 (both 2), then 436, 839 (both 3), then 355, 457, 657 (all 5):
$$[720,\ 329,\ 436,\ 839,\ 355,\ 457,\ 657]$$

*Pass 3, hundreds digit:* digits are 7, 3, 4, 8, 3, 4, 6. Stable ordering gives 329, 355 (both 3), 436, 457 (both 4), 657 (6), 720 (7), 839 (8):
$$[329,\ 355,\ 436,\ 457,\ 657,\ 720,\ 839]$$

Sorted. Note that after pass 2, 329 precedes 355 purely because of the tens digit, and pass 3 preserves that relative order — that is stability doing the work. Cost: $d = 3$ passes over $n = 7$ items with $k = 10$ buckets, so $\Theta(d(n+k)) = 3 \times 17 = 51$ elementary steps, against roughly $7 \log_2 7 \approx 20$ comparisons for a comparison sort. Radix sort only pays off when $n$ is large relative to $d$ and $k$.
