blocks.text:
## Searching

**Linear search** costs $\Theta(n)$ worst case and $(n+1)/2$ comparisons on average for a successful search in an unsorted array. It is the only option for unsorted data or for linked lists.

**Binary search** on a sorted array halves the interval each step:

$$T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1) \;\Longrightarrow\; \Theta(\log n)$$

The maximum number of comparisons for a successful search among $n$ elements is $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$, and an unsuccessful search takes $\lfloor \log_2 n\rfloor + 1$ comparisons as well. For $n = 1000$ that is 10; for $n = 10^6$ it is 20. The **binary search tree** implied by the algorithm has the array midpoints as internal nodes, which is why questions sometimes ask you to draw it.

A vital precondition: **binary search requires random access**, so it is $\Theta(\log n)$ on an array and useless on a linked list, where reaching the midpoint already costs $\Theta(n)$.

**Interpolation search** guesses the position by linear interpolation between the endpoints instead of taking the midpoint:

$$\text{pos} = lo + \frac{(x - A[lo])\,(hi - lo)}{A[hi] - A[lo]}$$

On **uniformly distributed** data it runs in $O(\log\log n)$ expected time, which is why phone-book lookup feels instantaneous. On skewed data it degrades to $O(n)$ — strictly worse than binary search's guarantee.

**Jump search** on a sorted array steps forward in blocks of $\sqrt n$ and then searches linearly inside one block, costing $O(\sqrt n)$. It is the right answer when jumping backwards is expensive, as on tape.

**Ternary search** splits into three parts and needs about $2\log_3 n \approx 1.26 \log_2 n$ comparisons — **more** than binary search, not fewer. It is genuinely useful only for finding the extremum of a unimodal function, not for searching a sorted array.

**Selection — finding the $k$-th smallest.** Sorting first costs $\Theta(n\log n)$. `QUICKSELECT` (partition and recurse into one side only) gives $\Theta(n)$ expected and $\Theta(n^2)$ worst case. The **median-of-medians** algorithm, which chooses the pivot as the median of the medians of groups of 5, guarantees a split no worse than 30/70 and achieves $\Theta(n)$ in the **worst** case via $T(n) \le T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + \Theta(n)$. Using groups of 3 instead of 5 breaks the proof, because $T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + \Theta(n)$ is $\Theta(n\log n)$.

blocks.q: Which of the following sorting algorithms is stable, in place, and has $O(n)$ best-case running time?
blocks.exp: Insertion sort satisfies all three: equal keys are never swapped past each other (stable), only $O(1)$ extra space is used (in place), and on an already sorted array each element is compared once and moved zero times ($\Theta(n)$). Heapsort and quicksort are unstable; merge sort on arrays needs $\Theta(n)$ auxiliary space and has no sub-$n\log n$ best case.

blocks.q: Quicksort is applied to an array that is already sorted in ascending order, always choosing the **first** element as pivot. The running time is
blocks.exp: With the first element as pivot on ascending data, every partition puts zero elements on the left and $n-1$ on the right, so $T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(n)$, which unrolls to $\Theta(n^2)$. This is the standard reason for randomising the pivot: sorted or nearly sorted input is common in practice, so the 'unlikely' worst case would in fact happen constantly.

blocks.q: An array of $n$ elements is to be sorted using counting sort where the keys lie in the range $0$ to $n^3 - 1$. The best achievable running time is
blocks.exp: Counting sort is $\Theta(n + k)$ and here $k = n^3$, so it is $\Theta(n^3)$ — worse than a comparison sort. The right fix is radix sort: write each key in base $n$, which takes 3 digits, giving $\Theta(3(n + n)) = \Theta(n)$. The question as asked is about counting sort alone, so $\Theta(n^3)$.

tricks.title: Count inversions, not steps
tricks.body: The number of swaps in bubble sort and the number of shifts in insertion sort both equal the number of inversions exactly. Selection sort always does $n-1$ swaps regardless of the data. If a question asks for a swap count on a specific small array, count inversions instead of simulating.

tricks.title: $n\log_2 n - n + 1$ for merge sort comparisons
tricks.body: For $n$ a power of 2 this is the exact worst-case comparison count. For $n=8$ it is 17, for $n=16$ it is 49. If options include $n\log n$ exactly (24 and 64), they are the loose upper bound and the more precise figure is the intended answer when the question says 'maximum number of comparisons'.

tricks.title: Stable-and-not-in-place go together for the linear sorts
tricks.body: Counting, radix and bucket sort are all stable and all need $\Theta(n+k)$ extra space. The in-place sorts that are unstable are quicksort, heapsort, selection sort and shell sort. Only insertion and bubble sort are both stable and in place — that pair answers most 'which algorithm is both' questions.

tricks.title: Use the decision-tree bound to reject options
tricks.body: Any claim that a **comparison** sort runs in $o(n\log n)$ worst case is false by the $\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil$ bound. Any linear-time claim must come with a non-comparison mechanism (counting, radix, bucket) and a bounded key range.

tricks.title: Binary search comparison count is $\lfloor\log_2 n\rfloor + 1$
tricks.body: For $n = 100$ it is 7, for $n = 1000$ it is 10, for $n = 10^6$ it is 20. Learn those three anchors and interpolate; you will never need to run the algorithm.

traps.title: Selection sort has no good case
traps.body: It is $\Theta(n^2)$ on sorted, reverse-sorted and random input alike, because the minimum-finding scan is unconditional. Only its swap count (always $n-1$) is small. Options offering $\Theta(n)$ best case for selection sort are always wrong.

traps.title: Merge sort is in place on linked lists
traps.body: The $\Theta(n)$ space cost is an artefact of arrays. On a linked list the merge is done by relinking, so merge sort uses $O(\log n)$ stack and nothing else — which is why it, and not quicksort, is the standard list sort.

traps.title: Radix sort must go least-significant digit first
traps.body: MSD-first radix sort needs recursion into buckets to be correct; the simple loop version is LSD-first and depends completely on the inner sort being stable. 'Radix sort is stable' and 'radix sort processes the least significant digit first' are the same fact stated twice.

traps.title: Ternary search is not faster than binary search
traps.body: It makes about 1.26 times as many comparisons because each step does up to two comparisons to shrink by a factor of 3, and $2/\log_2 3 > 1/\log_2 2$. The intuition 'more splits must be faster' is exactly what the examiner is testing.

topics.title: Asymptotic Analysis and Recurrences
topics.summary: The five asymptotic notations, the growth-rate ladder, and the three techniques for recurrences with the Master theorem stated precisely and all three cases worked.

blocks.text:
## The five notations

Asymptotic notation describes how a function grows as $n \to \infty$, discarding constant factors and small $n$. Formally, for functions on the positive integers:

| Notation | Meaning | Definition | Loose analogy |
|---|---|---|---|
| $f = O(g)$ | upper bound | $\exists c>0, n_0: 0 \le f(n) \le c\,g(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$ | $f \le g$ |
| $f = \Omega(g)$ | lower bound | $\exists c>0, n_0: 0 \le c\,g(n) \le f(n)$ for all $n \ge n_0$ | $f \ge g$ |
| $f = \Theta(g)$ | tight bound | both of the above | $f = g$ |
| $f = o(g)$ | strict upper | $\forall c>0\ \exists n_0: f(n) < c\,g(n)$ for $n \ge n_0$; i.e. $f/g \to 0$ | $f < g$ |
| $f = \omega(g)$ | strict lower | $g/f \to 0$ | $f > g$ |

Properties worth having ready:

- **Transitivity** holds for all five. **Reflexivity** holds for $O$, $\Omega$, $\Theta$ but not for $o$, $\omega$ ($f \ne o(f)$).
- **Symmetry**: $f = \Theta(g) \iff g = \Theta(f)$. **Transpose symmetry**: $f = O(g) \iff g = \Omega(f)$, and $f = o(g) \iff g = \omega(f)$.
- $\Theta(g) = O(g) \cap \Omega(g)$.
- $f_1 = O(g_1)$ and $f_2 = O(g_2)$ imply $f_1 + f_2 = O(\max(g_1,g_2))$ and $f_1 f_2 = O(g_1 g_2)$.
- **The trichotomy of real numbers does not carry over.** There exist $f, g$ with $f \ne O(g)$ and $f \ne \Omega(g)$ — for example $f(n) = n$ and $g(n) = n^{1+\sin n}$.

$O$ is an upper bound, not necessarily a tight one: $n = O(n^{100})$ is a true statement. So "the worst-case running time of merge sort is $O(n^2)$" is **true** but uninformative, and an exam option saying so is usually correct rather than wrong. Read the question's wording carefully: "tight bound" means $\Theta$.

## The growth ladder

From slowest to fastest growing, for $\varepsilon > 0$ and $c > 1$:

$$1 \prec \log\log n \prec \log n \prec (\log n)^k \prec n^{\varepsilon} \prec n \prec n\log n \prec n^2 \prec n^3 \prec n^{\log n} \prec c^{\,n} \prec n! \prec n^n$$

Three identities that turn up constantly:

- $\log(n!) = \Theta(n\log n)$ by Stirling, so a comparison sort's decision-tree bound is $\Omega(n\log n)$.
- $\sum_{i=1}^n 1/i = H_n = \Theta(\log n)$ — the harmonic series, which is where the $\log n$ in randomised quicksort and in hashing analyses comes from.
- $a^{\log_b n} = n^{\log_b a}$, the identity that makes the Master theorem work.

Also note that the base of a logarithm is a constant factor, so $\Theta(\log_2 n) = \Theta(\log_{10} n) = \Theta(\ln n)$ and writing the base inside $\Theta$ is pointless. But the base of an **exponential** matters enormously: $2^n$ and $3^n$ are not the same class, since $3^n/2^n = 1.5^n \to \infty$.

To compare two unfamiliar functions, take logarithms. For example, is $n^{\log n}$ bigger than $2^n$? Compare $\log^2 n$ against $n\log 2$: the second wins for large $n$, so $2^n$ grows faster.

## Three ways to solve a recurrence

### 1. Substitution (guess and verify)
Guess the form of the answer and prove it by induction, solving for the constants. To show $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$ is $O(n\log n)$, assume $T(k) \le c\,k\log_2 k$ for all $k < n$; then

$$T(n) \le 2\,c\,\frac n2 \log_2 \frac n2 + n = c\,n(\log_2 n - 1) + n = c\,n\log_2 n - cn + n \le c\,n\log_2 n$$

whenever $c \ge 1$. The base case is handled by choosing $n_0 = 2$ and $c$ large enough to cover $T(2)$ and $T(3)$ — you cannot use $n = 1$ because $\log_2 1 = 0$.

The characteristic failure of substitution is proving a bound that is *almost* right and finding the induction does not close; the fix is to **strengthen the hypothesis by subtracting a lower-order term**, e.g. guess $T(n) \le cn - d$ rather than $T(n) \le cn$.

### 2. Recursion tree
Draw the tree of recursive calls, compute the total work per level, and sum over levels. This is the fastest way to *find* the answer, which you can then verify by substitution if the question demands rigour.

For $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n$: level $i$ has $2^i$ nodes each doing $n/2^i$ work, so every level costs $n$; the tree has $\log_2 n + 1$ levels; total $\Theta(n\log n)$.

For the unbalanced $T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n$: every level still costs $n$, but the depths of the shallowest and deepest paths are $\log_3 n$ and $\log_{3/2} n$, both $\Theta(\log n)$, so the answer is again $\Theta(n\log n)$ — with a constant hidden inside.

### 3. Iteration / back-substitution
Expand the recurrence repeatedly until a pattern appears, then sum. For $T(n) = T(n-1) + n$, $T(1) = 1$:

$$T(n) = n + (n-1) + (n-2) + \cdots + 1 = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} = \Theta(n^2)$$

For $T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1$, $T(0)=0$: expanding gives $2^n - 1$, which is the Tower of Hanoi count.

blocks.title: The Master theorem, stated precisely
blocks.text:
For the recurrence

$$T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + f(n), \qquad a \ge 1,\ b > 1,\ f(n) > 0$$

compare $f(n)$ against the **watershed function** $n^{\log_b a}$.

**Case 1.** If $f(n) = O\!\left(n^{\log_b a - \varepsilon}\right)$ for some constant $\varepsilon > 0$ — that is, $f$ is *polynomially smaller* — then
$$T(n) = \Theta\!\left(n^{\log_b a}\right)$$
The leaves dominate.

**Case 2.** If $f(n) = \Theta\!\left(n^{\log_b a}\log^k n\right)$ for some constant $k \ge 0$, then
$$T(n) = \Theta\!\left(n^{\log_b a}\log^{k+1} n\right)$$
Every level costs the same, so you gain one logarithm.

**Case 3.** If $f(n) = \Omega\!\left(n^{\log_b a + \varepsilon}\right)$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$ — *polynomially larger* — **and** the regularity condition
$$a\,f(n/b) \le c\,f(n) \quad \text{for some } c < 1 \text{ and all sufficiently large } n$$
holds, then
$$T(n) = \Theta(f(n))$$
The root dominates.

**The gaps.** The word *polynomially* is not decoration. If $f$ is smaller or larger than $n^{\log_b a}$ by only a logarithmic factor that Case 2 does not cover, no case applies. The standard example is
$$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \frac{n}{\log n}$$
where $n^{\log_b a} = n$ and $f(n) = n/\log n$ is smaller by a factor of $\log n$ — not by any $n^{\varepsilon}$. The true answer, obtained by a recursion tree and the harmonic series, is $\Theta(n\log\log n)$.

Case 3's regularity condition can also fail, as for $T(n) = T(n/2) + n(2 - \cos n)$.

blocks.title: Worked example — all three Master cases and two that fail
blocks.text:
**Case 1.** $T(n) = 8T(n/2) + 1000n^2$.
$\log_b a = \log_2 8 = 3$, so the watershed is $n^3$. Is $f(n) = 1000n^2 = O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$? Yes, with $\varepsilon = 1$. **Case 1**, so $T(n) = \Theta(n^3)$.

**Case 2, $k=0$.** $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 10n$.
$\log_2 2 = 1$, watershed $n^1$. $f(n) = 10n = \Theta(n^1\log^0 n)$. **Case 2 with $k = 0$**, so $T(n) = \Theta(n\log n)$. This is merge sort.

**Case 2, $k=1$.** $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n\log n$.
Watershed is still $n$. $f(n) = n\log n = \Theta(n^1 \log^1 n)$, so $k = 1$ and $T(n) = \Theta(n\log^2 n)$. Note this is *not* Case 3: $n\log n$ is **not** $\Omega(n^{1+\varepsilon})$ for any positive $\varepsilon$, because $\log n$ grows slower than every $n^{\varepsilon}$.

**Case 3.** $T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n\log n$.
$\log_4 3 = 0.7925$, watershed $n^{0.7925}$. Is $f(n) = n\log n = \Omega(n^{0.7925 + \varepsilon})$? Yes — take $\varepsilon = 0.2$, since $n\log n$ beats $n^{0.9925}$. Regularity: $a f(n/b) = 3 \cdot \frac n4 \log\frac n4 \le \frac34 n\log n = c\,f(n)$ with $c = 3/4 < 1$. **Case 3**, so $T(n) = \Theta(n\log n)$.

**Case 1 with a fractional exponent.** $T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n^2$ — Strassen's recurrence.
$\log_2 7 = 2.807$, watershed $n^{2.807}$. $f(n) = n^2 = O(n^{2.807 - 0.8})$, so **Case 1** and $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 7}) = \Theta(n^{2.807})$.

**No case applies (gap below).** $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n/\log n$.
Watershed $n$; $f(n) = n/\log n$ is asymptotically smaller but only by $\log n$, and $n/\log n \ne O(n^{1-\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$. Recursion tree: level $i$ has $2^i$ subproblems of size $n/2^i$ each costing $\dfrac{n/2^i}{\log(n/2^i)}$, so level $i$ costs $\dfrac{n}{\log n - i}$. Summing $i = 0$ to $\log_2 n - 1$ gives $n\sum_{j=1}^{\log_2 n} \frac1j = n\,H_{\log_2 n} = \Theta(n\log\log n)$.

**No case applies (regularity fails).** $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n^2(2 + \sin n)$. The amplitude oscillates, so $a f(n/b) \le c f(n)$ cannot be made to hold for a single $c < 1$ at every large $n$, even though $f$ is polynomially larger than the watershed $n$.

## Recurrences the Master theorem cannot touch

**Subtract-and-conquer**, $T(n) = a\,T(n-b) + f(n)$ with $a \ge 1$, $b > 0$ and $f(n) = \Theta(n^k)$:

$$T(n) = \begin{cases}\Theta(n^k) & a < 1\\[2pt] \Theta(n^{k+1}) & a = 1\\[2pt] \Theta\!\left(n^k\,a^{n/b}\right) & a > 1\end{cases}$$

So $T(n) = T(n-1) + 1$ is $\Theta(n)$; $T(n) = T(n-1) + n$ is $\Theta(n^2)$; $T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1$ is $\Theta(2^n)$.

**Change of variable.** For $T(n) = 2T(\sqrt n) + \log n$, substitute $n = 2^m$ and $S(m) = T(2^m)$:

$$S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m \;\Longrightarrow\; S(m) = \Theta(m\log m) \;\Longrightarrow\; T(n) = \Theta(\log n\,\log\log n)$$

Similarly $T(n) = T(\sqrt n) + 1$ becomes $S(m) = S(m/2) + 1 = \Theta(\log m)$, so $T(n) = \Theta(\log\log n)$ — this is the recurrence behind interpolation search and the van Emde Boas tree.

**Linear recurrences with constant coefficients** such as $T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2)$ are solved by the characteristic equation: $x^2 = x + 1$ gives $x = \frac{1\pm\sqrt5}{2}$, so $T(n) = \Theta(\phi^n)$ with $\phi = 1.618$. That is why naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential.

**Akra–Bazzi** generalises the Master theorem to unequal splits such as $T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n$; you are not expected to apply it, only to recognise that the Master theorem does not cover unequal splits.

blocks.q: The solution of $T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n^2\log n$ is
blocks.exp: Here $\log_b a = \log_2 4 = 2$, so the watershed is $n^2$ and $f(n) = n^2\log n = \Theta(n^2\log^1 n)$. That is Case 2 with $k = 1$, which adds one logarithm: $T(n) = \Theta(n^2\log^{2} n)$. It is not Case 3, because $n^2\log n$ is not $\Omega(n^{2+\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$.

blocks.q: Which statement is true?
blocks.exp: $2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n$, a constant multiple, so it is $O(2^n)$. But $2^{2n} = (2^n)^2$, and the ratio $2^{2n}/2^n = 2^n$ is unbounded, so no constant $c$ works. Constants in the *exponent* are not constant factors — that is the whole point of this classic item.

blocks.q: For which recurrence does the Master theorem fail to apply?
blocks.exp: In option 3 the watershed is $n^{\log_2 2} = n$, and $n/\log n$ is smaller than $n$ but not by any polynomial factor $n^{\varepsilon}$, so it falls between Case 1 and Case 2 — no case applies, and the true answer $\Theta(n\log\log n)$ needs a recursion tree. The others are clean: Case 3 ($\Theta(n^3)$), Case 1 ($\Theta(n^2)$), and Case 2 with $k=1$ ($\Theta(n^2\log^2 n)$).

tricks.title: Compute $n^{\log_b a}$ first, always
tricks.body: Write down $\log_b a$ before looking at $f(n)$. Then one glance settles the case: $f$ smaller by a power gives the watershed, $f$ equal (up to $\log^k$) gives the watershed times one more log, $f$ bigger by a power gives $f$. Handy values: $\log_2 3 = 1.585$, $\log_2 7 = 2.807$, $\log_3 2 = 0.631$, $\log_4 3 = 0.792$.

tricks.title: $\log^k n$ never beats $n^{\varepsilon}$
tricks.body: Whenever $f(n)$ differs from $n^{\log_b a}$ only by logarithms, you are in Case 2 (if the power of $\log$ is non-negative) or in the gap (if it is negative). Never call $n\log n$ 'polynomially larger' than $n$ — that single misjudgement produces the wrong answer on a large fraction of Master-theorem questions.

tricks.title: The recursion tree gives the answer in ten seconds
tricks.body: Work per level is $a^i f(n/b^i)$. If that decreases geometrically the root dominates; if it increases geometrically the leaves dominate (there are $n^{\log_b a}$ of them); if it is constant, multiply by the number of levels $\log_b n$. This is the Master theorem, derived rather than remembered.

tricks.title: Substitute $n = 2^m$ for square-root recurrences
tricks.body: Any recurrence with $T(\sqrt n)$ becomes a standard divide-by-2 recurrence under $n = 2^m$. Solve in $m$, then back-substitute $m = \log n$. $T(\sqrt n)+1 \to \Theta(\log\log n)$; $2T(\sqrt n)+\log n \to \Theta(\log n \log\log n)$.

tricks.title: $T(n-1)$ means multiply, $T(n/2)$ means logarithm
tricks.body: A recurrence that subtracts has $n$ levels, so a $\Theta(n^k)$ cost per level gives $\Theta(n^{k+1})$ when $a=1$ and an exponential when $a \ge 2$. A recurrence that divides has $\log_b n$ levels. Identifying which family you are in before anything else prevents applying the Master theorem where it does not belong.

traps.title: $O$ is an upper bound, not the running time
traps.body: 'Insertion sort is $O(n^2)$' and 'insertion sort is $O(n^3)$' are both true. When a question asks which statements are correct, do not reject a loose but valid bound. Only $\Theta$ claims can be wrong for being too loose.

traps.title: Case 3 needs the regularity condition
traps.body: Showing $f(n) = \Omega(n^{\log_b a + \varepsilon})$ is not enough on its own. You must also have $a f(n/b) \le c f(n)$ for some $c < 1$. For every polynomial $f$ it holds automatically, which is why it is usually skipped — but a question that supplies an oscillating or unusual $f$ is testing exactly this.

traps.title: $\Theta$ of an average case is not $\Theta$ of the worst case
traps.body: Quicksort's average is $\Theta(n\log n)$ and its worst is $\Theta(n^2)$; both are correct statements about the same algorithm. Always read whether the question says best, average or worst before choosing.

traps.title: Number of levels is $\log_b n$, not $\log_2 n$
traps.body: For $T(n) = 3T(n/4)+n$ the tree has $\log_4 n$ levels, not $\log_2 n$. Inside $\Theta$ the base does not matter, but it very much matters when a question asks for an exact level count or an exact number of leaves ($a^{\log_b n} = n^{\log_b a}$).

topics.title: Divide and Conquer
topics.summary: The paradigm and its recurrence signature, with binary search, merge sort, Strassen, Karatsuba, closest pair, quickselect and inversion counting worked through.

blocks.text:
## The paradigm

Divide and conquer solves a problem in three steps:

1. **Divide** the instance into $a$ subproblems, each of size roughly $n/b$.
2. **Conquer** each subproblem by recursion, stopping at a base case small enough to solve directly.
3. **Combine** the subsolutions into a solution for the original instance.

The running time is therefore always of the form $T(n) = a\,T(n/b) + D(n) + C(n)$, where $D$ is the cost of dividing and $C$ the cost of combining — which is exactly the shape the Master theorem handles. Recognising the values of $a$, $b$ and $f(n) = D(n)+C(n)$ for a described algorithm is the single most common question type in this topic.

Divide and conquer wins when the combine step is **cheaper than the work it saves**. Merge sort's combine is $\Theta(n)$, and that $\Theta(n)$ per level across $\log n$ levels is much less than the $\Theta(n^2)$ of insertion sort. Strassen's combine is more expensive than the naive one (18 matrix additions instead of 4), yet it wins because it does 7 recursive multiplications instead of 8, changing the *exponent*.

Two properties distinguish divide and conquer from dynamic programming: its subproblems are **independent and non-overlapping**, so nothing needs to be stored and reused; and it is naturally top-down and recursive, so it parallelises easily.

## The standard algorithms and their recurrences

| Algorithm | Recurrence | Solution |
|---|---|---|
| Binary search | $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1)$ | $\Theta(\log n)$ |
| Finding max and min | $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 2$ | $\Theta(n)$, exactly $\lceil 3n/2\rceil - 2$ comparisons |
| Merge sort | $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ |
| Quicksort (balanced) | $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ |
| Quicksort (worst) | $T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ |
| Quickselect (expected) | $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n)$ |
| Median of medians | $T(n) \le T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n)$ worst case |
| Naive matrix multiply (block) | $T(n) = 8T(n/2) + \Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n^3)$ |
| Strassen | $T(n) = 7T(n/2) + \Theta(n^2)$ | $\Theta(n^{\log_2 7}) = \Theta(n^{2.807})$ |
| Karatsuba integer multiply | $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n^{\log_2 3}) = \Theta(n^{1.585})$ |
| Closest pair of points | $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ |
| Maximum subarray (D&C) | $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ |
| Counting inversions | $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ |
| Tower of Hanoi | $T(n) = 2T(n-1) + 1$ | $2^n - 1$ moves |
| Fast exponentiation | $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1)$ | $\Theta(\log n)$ multiplications |
| Convex hull (divide and conquer) | $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ | $\Theta(n\log n)$ |

**Why the sum of subproblem sizes matters.** In median-of-medians the two recursive sizes add to $n/5 + 7n/10 = 9n/10 < n$, so the geometric series converges and the total is $\Theta(n)$. With groups of 3 the sizes would be $n/3 + 2n/3 = n$, the series does not converge, and the algorithm becomes $\Theta(n\log n)$. That single inequality is the reason the constant 5 appears.

## Strassen's algorithm

To multiply two $n \times n$ matrices, split each into four $n/2 \times n/2$ blocks. The naive block method computes each of the four result blocks as a sum of two block products — 8 multiplications and 4 additions of $n/2$-sized blocks — giving $T(n) = 8T(n/2) + \Theta(n^2) = \Theta(n^3)$, no better than the triple loop.

Strassen forms **seven** cleverly chosen products $M_1 \ldots M_7$, each of a *sum or difference* of blocks, and recovers the four result blocks by adding and subtracting those seven products. The count of block additions and subtractions rises from 4 to 18, but additions cost $\Theta(n^2)$ and do not change the exponent, whereas multiplications do:

$$T(n) = 7T(n/2) + \Theta(n^2), \qquad \log_2 7 = 2.807 \;\Longrightarrow\; T(n) = \Theta(n^{2.807})$$

Points examiners test: **7 multiplications and 18 additions/subtractions**; the crossover against the naive algorithm is around $n \approx 100$ because of the large constant; Strassen is numerically less stable; and it needs $\Theta(n^2)$ extra space for the intermediate matrices. Later algorithms have pushed the exponent below 2.4, and the trivial lower bound is $\Omega(n^2)$ since every entry must be read.

**Karatsuba** is the same idea for integers. Writing $x = x_1 B + x_0$ and $y = y_1 B + y_0$ with $B = 10^{n/2}$, the product needs $x_1y_1$, $x_0y_0$ and the cross terms; Karatsuba gets the cross terms from a **third** product $(x_1+x_0)(y_1+y_0) - x_1y_1 - x_0y_0$, so three multiplications instead of four:

$$T(n) = 3T(n/2) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 3}) = \Theta(n^{1.585})$$

blocks.title: Worked example — counting inversions by merging
blocks.text:
Count the inversions in $A = [2, 4, 1, 3, 5]$, that is, pairs $(i,j)$ with $i<j$ and $A[i] > A[j]$.

**By hand, to have a target:** $(2,1)$, $(4,1)$, $(4,3)$ — **3 inversions**.

**By divide and conquer.** Split into $L = [2,4,1]$ and $R = [3,5]$; total inversions = inversions within $L$ + inversions within $R$ + inversions spanning the split.

*Left half $[2,4,1]$.* Split into $[2]$ and $[4,1]$. Inside $[4,1]$: merging $[4]$ with $[1]$, the element 1 is taken from the right while one element (4) remains on the left, contributing **1** inversion; the sorted result is $[1,4]$. Now merge $[2]$ with $[1,4]$: take 1 from the right while 1 element remains on the left $\to$ **+1**; take 2 from the left; take 4 from the right with nothing left $\to$ +0. Sorted left half $[1,2,4]$, inversions so far in $L$: $1+1 = 2$.

*Right half $[3,5]$.* Already sorted, **0** inversions.

*Merging $[1,2,4]$ with $[3,5]$.* Compare 1 vs 3: take 1 (left, no inversion). 2 vs 3: take 2. 4 vs 3: take **3 from the right** while 1 element (4) remains on the left $\to$ **+1**. 4 vs 5: take 4. Take 5. Split inversions: **1**.

**Total: $2 + 0 + 1 = 3$.** Matches the hand count.

The key insight is the counting rule: **when an element is taken from the right half during a merge, add the number of elements still remaining in the left half**, because each of them is larger and sits earlier. The merge is $\Theta(n)$ as usual, so $T(n) = 2T(n/2)+\Theta(n) = \Theta(n\log n)$ — far better than the $\Theta(n^2)$ of checking every pair.

**A second calculation for contrast — binary search comparison count.** A sorted array of 1000 elements: the recurrence $T(n) = T(n/2)+1$ gives $\lfloor\log_2 1000\rfloor + 1 = 9 + 1 = 10$ comparisons in the worst case. Doubling the array to 2000 adds exactly one comparison, which is the practical meaning of a logarithm.

## Closest pair of points

Given $n$ points in the plane, find the two closest. Brute force is $\Theta(n^2)$; divide and conquer achieves $\Theta(n\log n)$.

Presort the points by $x$ (once, $\Theta(n\log n)$). Then recursively:

1. Split by the vertical line at the median $x$ into left and right halves of $n/2$ points each.
2. Recursively find the closest pair in each half; let $d = \min(d_L, d_R)$.
3. **Combine:** the only pairs not yet considered are those straddling the line, and such a pair can beat $d$ only if both points lie in the vertical strip of width $2d$ centred on the line. Sort the strip's points by $y$ (or merge, keeping a $y$-sorted list as you return) and, for each point in the strip, compare it against only the **next 7 points** in $y$ order.

The constant 7 comes from packing: a $d \times 2d$ rectangle can hold at most 8 points that are pairwise at least $d$ apart, so beyond the 7th neighbour every point is already further than $d$ away. That makes the combine step $\Theta(n)$, giving $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n) = \Theta(n\log n)$. Without the $y$-merge — re-sorting the strip at every level — the recurrence becomes $2T(n/2) + \Theta(n\log n) = \Theta(n\log^2 n)$, which is the answer if a question describes that version.

## Where divide and conquer is the wrong tool

If the subproblems **overlap**, plain recursion recomputes the same values exponentially often. Naive recursive Fibonacci is $T(n) = T(n-1)+T(n-2)+\Theta(1) = \Theta(\phi^n)$ for exactly this reason. The cure is memoisation, which turns the algorithm into dynamic programming — that is the precise boundary between the two paradigms, and topic 7.8 develops it.

blocks.q: An algorithm divides a problem of size $n$ into 5 subproblems of size $n/2$ each and combines the results in $\Theta(n)$ time. Its running time is
blocks.exp: $T(n) = 5T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$, so $\log_b a = \log_2 5 \approx 2.32$. Since $f(n) = n = O(n^{2.32-\varepsilon})$, Master Case 1 applies and $T(n) = \Theta(n^{\log_2 5}) \approx \Theta(n^{2.32})$. The leaves dominate whenever the branching factor outruns the shrink factor.

blocks.q: Strassen's algorithm improves on the $\Theta(n^3)$ block method because it
blocks.exp: Both methods split into four $n/2 \times n/2$ blocks. The naive one needs 8 recursive multiplications, Strassen only 7, at the cost of rising from 4 to 18 additions. Since additions are $\Theta(n^2)$ they do not affect the exponent, while the multiplication count sits in the recurrence's $a$: $\log_2 8 = 3$ becomes $\log_2 7 = 2.807$.

blocks.q: Why does the median-of-medians selection algorithm use groups of 5 rather than groups of 3?
opts: Groups of 3 give a pivot that is not a median
With groups of 3 the recursive sizes sum to at least $n$, so the recursion is not linear
Groups of 5 minimise the number of comparisons per group
Groups of 3 cannot be sorted in constant time
blocks.exp: With groups of 5 the recurrence is $T(n) \le T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + \Theta(n)$ and $1/5 + 7/10 = 9/10 < 1$, so the work decreases geometrically and totals $\Theta(n)$. With groups of 3 the pivot guarantee weakens to $T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + \Theta(n)$, whose sizes sum to exactly $n$, and that recurrence solves to $\Theta(n\log n)$.

tricks.title: Read $a$, $b$ and $f$ straight off the description
tricks.body: 'Divides into $a$ subproblems of size $n/b$ and combines in $f(n)$' is literally the Master theorem's input. Most divide-and-conquer questions are Master-theorem questions in disguise and need no knowledge of the specific algorithm.

tricks.title: Number of leaves is $n^{\log_b a}$
tricks.body: A tree with branching $a$ and depth $\log_b n$ has $a^{\log_b n} = n^{\log_b a}$ leaves. This gives Case 1's answer instantly and explains why reducing $a$ from 8 to 7 changes the exponent while reducing the combine cost does not.

tricks.title: Check whether the subproblem sizes sum to less than $n$
tricks.body: For unequal splits $T(n) = T(\alpha n)+T(\beta n)+\Theta(n)$: if $\alpha+\beta < 1$ the answer is $\Theta(n)$; if $\alpha + \beta = 1$ it is $\Theta(n\log n)$; if $\alpha+\beta>1$ it is superlinear. This one test answers median-of-medians, quickselect and their variants.

tricks.title: Tower of Hanoi numbers: $2^n - 1$ moves, disk $k$ moves $2^{n-k}$ times
tricks.body: The total is $2^n-1$; the largest disk moves once; the smallest moves $2^{n-1}$ times, i.e. on every alternate move. Questions asking 'which disk is moved at step $m$' are answered by the number of trailing zeros in the binary form of $m$.

tricks.title: Exponents worth memorising
tricks.body: $\log_2 3 = 1.585$ (Karatsuba, and the $3T(n/2)$ family), $\log_2 7 = 2.807$ (Strassen), $\log_2 5 = 2.322$, $\log_3 2 = 0.631$. Recognising these immediately identifies which classic algorithm a disguised recurrence refers to.

traps.title: Divide and conquer requires independent subproblems
traps.body: If the subproblems share work, recursion is exponential and the correct paradigm is dynamic programming. 'Divide and conquer with overlapping subproblems' describes no real algorithm — that phrase in an option is a distractor.

traps.title: More subproblems is not better
traps.body: The intuition that splitting into more pieces speeds things up is backwards: $a$ appears in the *exponent* $n^{\log_b a}$. Splitting into 4 halves instead of 2 turns $\Theta(n\log n)$ into $\Theta(n^2)$.

traps.title: Presorting is part of the closest-pair bound
traps.body: The clean $\Theta(n\log n)$ requires sorting by $x$ once outside the recursion and maintaining $y$-order by merging. Re-sorting the strip inside every call gives $\Theta(n\log^2 n)$. Which figure is correct depends on the version the question describes.

traps.title: Quicksort's average case is not a Master-theorem Case 2
traps.body: The recurrence $T(n) = T(n/10)+T(9n/10)+\Theta(n)$ that models a lopsided-but-constant split is an unequal split, outside the Master theorem's scope. It solves to $\Theta(n\log n)$ by a recursion tree, not by quoting the theorem.

topics.title: Greedy Algorithms
topics.summary: The greedy-choice property, activity selection, fractional knapsack, Huffman coding and job sequencing — and precisely why greedy fails for 0/1 knapsack and for coin systems.

blocks.text:
## What makes an algorithm greedy

A greedy algorithm builds a solution one decision at a time, always taking the option that looks best **right now**, and never revisiting a decision. That is all. The interesting question is never how to be greedy; it is whether being greedy is correct.

Greedy is provably correct exactly when the problem has two properties:

**Greedy-choice property.** Some optimal solution contains the locally best choice. The proof technique is always an **exchange argument**: take any optimal solution, show that swapping in the greedy choice does not make it worse, and conclude that an optimal solution exists that agrees with greedy on the first decision. Induct.

**Optimal substructure.** After the greedy choice is fixed, an optimal solution to the remaining subproblem, combined with that choice, is optimal for the whole.

Dynamic programming needs optimal substructure too, but not the greedy-choice property; that is the entire difference between the paradigms. Greedy makes its choice **before** solving subproblems and therefore solves only one subproblem per step, which is why it is usually $O(n\log n)$ — the cost of the sort that orders the choices. Dynamic programming makes its choice **after** solving all relevant subproblems, so it solves many, which is why it is usually polynomial in a table dimension.

A greedy algorithm that is not provably optimal can still be a useful **heuristic** or **approximation algorithm** — the 2-approximation for vertex cover and the nearest-neighbour tour for TSP are both greedy and both wrong in general, but bounded.

## Activity selection

Given $n$ activities with start and finish times $(s_i, f_i)$, select the largest set of mutually non-overlapping activities.

**The correct greedy rule is earliest finishing time first.** Sort by $f_i$ ascending, take the first activity, then repeatedly take the next activity whose start time is $\ge$ the finish time of the last one selected. Total cost $O(n\log n)$ for the sort and $O(n)$ for the scan.

Why it works: among all activities compatible with what has been chosen, the one that finishes earliest leaves the largest possible amount of time free for everything after it. Formally, if an optimal solution starts with activity $x$ and greedy would pick $g$ with $f_g \le f_x$, replacing $x$ by $g$ in the optimal solution keeps it feasible and the same size.

Three rules that **do not** work, each a standard distractor:

- **Shortest duration first.** A short activity can straddle the boundary between two long compatible ones, blocking both.
- **Earliest start time first.** One activity that starts at time 0 and runs all day blocks everything.
- **Fewest conflicts first.** Plausible, but constructible counterexamples exist.

The **interval-partitioning** variant — schedule all activities using the fewest rooms — has a different greedy rule: sort by *start* time and assign each activity to any free room, opening a new one when none is free. The number of rooms needed equals the maximum number of activities overlapping at any instant (the "depth"), and the greedy achieves it.

## Knapsack: where greedy works and where it fails

**Fractional knapsack.** Items have weight $w_i$ and value $v_i$; the knapsack holds $W$; items may be cut. Sort by value density $v_i/w_i$ descending and fill greedily, taking a fraction of the last item that fits. This is **optimal**, and the exchange argument is immediate: if any optimal solution contains a unit of weight of a lower-density item while a higher-density item is not fully taken, swapping that unit increases the value.

**0/1 knapsack.** The same items, but each must be taken whole or left. **Greedy by density is not optimal.** The fractional argument collapses the instant you cannot swap a *unit of weight*, because the item you would like to swap in may not fit at all.

Nor does any other simple rule rescue it. Greedy by value alone fails (a single heavy high-value item can exclude several better ones); greedy by weight alone fails (many cheap light items can exclude one valuable one). 0/1 knapsack is NP-complete, so no polynomial greedy rule can be correct unless P = NP. It is solved in topic 7.8 by dynamic programming in $O(nW)$ — pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial.

**The counterexample to keep.** Capacity $W = 8$, items

| Item | $w_i$ | $v_i$ | density $v_i/w_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 3 | 1.50 |
| 2 | 3 | 4 | 1.33 |
| 3 | 4 | 5 | 1.25 |
| 4 | 5 | 6 | 1.20 |

Greedy by density takes item 1 (weight used 2), then item 2 (weight used 5), then finds item 3 needs 4 and only 3 remains, and item 4 needs 5 — both rejected. **Greedy value = 7.** The optimal 0/1 solution is items 2 and 4: weight $3+5 = 8$ exactly, **value 10**. Greedy loses 30%. (The fractional optimum, for comparison, is $3 + 4 + \tfrac34 \times 5 = 10.75$, and note it is an upper bound on the 0/1 optimum — a fact branch and bound exploits in topic 7.9.)

## Huffman coding

Huffman's algorithm builds an optimal **prefix-free** binary code for a set of symbols with given frequencies. Prefix-free means no codeword is a prefix of another, so the encoded stream decodes uniquely with no separators, simply by walking the tree from the root.

The algorithm: put every symbol in a min-priority queue keyed by frequency; repeatedly extract the two smallest, make them the children of a new internal node whose frequency is their sum, and insert that node; stop when one node remains. With a binary heap this is $O(n\log n)$; if the frequencies are already sorted, two queues give $O(n)$.

Facts examiners use:

- The tree is a **full** binary tree: every internal node has exactly 2 children, so with $n$ symbols there are $n-1$ internal nodes and $2n-1$ nodes in total, and the algorithm runs $n-1$ merge steps.
- The **two least frequent symbols** are always siblings at the maximum depth. That is the greedy-choice property, proved by exchange.
- The **most frequent symbol** gets the shortest codeword.
- The total encoded length equals $\sum_i f_i \cdot d_i$ where $d_i$ is the depth, which also equals the **sum of all internal node values** — a much faster way to compute it.
- Huffman codes are not unique (swapping the 0/1 labels of any node, or breaking ties differently, gives another optimal code), but the **total length is unique**.
- With equal frequencies, Huffman degenerates to a fixed-length code.
- Huffman is optimal among symbol-by-symbol codes; arithmetic coding beats it because it is not restricted to an integer number of bits per symbol.

The same algorithm solves the **optimal merge pattern** problem: merging sorted files of sizes $f_1 \ldots f_n$ two at a time, the minimum total number of record movements is obtained by always merging the two smallest files, and the answer is again the sum of the internal node values.

blocks.title: Worked example — Huffman code and encoded length
blocks.text:
Symbols and frequencies (per 100 characters): $a{:}45$, $b{:}13$, $c{:}12$, $d{:}16$, $e{:}9$, $f{:}5$.

**Merge steps** (always the two smallest):

| Step | Combine | New node | Queue after |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $f{:}5$ and $e{:}9$ | 14 | 12, 13, 14, 16, 45 |
| 2 | $c{:}12$ and $b{:}13$ | 25 | 14, 16, 25, 45 |
| 3 | $14$ and $d{:}16$ | 30 | 25, 30, 45 |
| 4 | $25$ and $30$ | 55 | 45, 55 |
| 5 | $45$ and $55$ | 100 | 100 |

Five merges for six symbols, as expected ($n-1$).

**Reading the depths from the tree.** The root (100) has children $a$ (45) and the 55-node. The 55-node has children 25 and 30. The 25-node has children $c$ and $b$. The 30-node has children the 14-node and $d$. The 14-node has children $f$ and $e$.

| Symbol | Depth | Codeword (left = 0) | $f_i \times d_i$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $a$ | 1 | `0` | $45 \times 1 = 45$ |
| $c$ | 3 | `100` | $12 \times 3 = 36$ |
| $b$ | 3 | `101` | $13 \times 3 = 39$ |
| $d$ | 3 | `111` | $16 \times 3 = 48$ |
| $f$ | 4 | `1100` | $5 \times 4 = 20$ |
| $e$ | 4 | `1101` | $9 \times 4 = 36$ |

**Total encoded length $= 45+36+39+48+20+36 = 224$ bits**, so the average code length is $224/100 = 2.24$ bits per symbol.

**Check by the internal-node shortcut:** sum of the internal node values $= 14 + 25 + 30 + 55 + 100 = 224$. Same answer, five additions instead of six multiplications.

**Compare with fixed-length coding:** six symbols need $\lceil\log_2 6\rceil = 3$ bits each, so 300 bits. Huffman saves 25.3%. The entropy lower bound is $-\sum p_i\log_2 p_i = 2.23$ bits, so Huffman is within 0.01 bits of optimal here.

**A tie-breaking note.** At step 2 the queue held 12, 13, 14, 16. Taking 12 and 13 is forced. But had the queue held 14, 14, 16, either 14 could have been chosen; different choices produce different codeword assignments with the same total of 224.

blocks.text:
## Job sequencing with deadlines

Each job $i$ has a profit $p_i$ and a deadline $d_i$; every job takes one unit of time; a job earns its profit only if it completes by its deadline. Maximise total profit on a single machine.

Greedy rule: **sort jobs by profit descending**, and schedule each job in the **latest free slot at or before its deadline**. Scheduling late leaves the early slots open for jobs with tight deadlines. With a simple array the cost is $O(n^2)$; with disjoint sets (union-find over slots) it is $O(n\,\alpha(n))$.

**Worked instance.** Jobs $(p, d)$: $J_1(20,2)$, $J_2(15,2)$, $J_3(10,1)$, $J_4(5,3)$, $J_5(1,3)$. Maximum deadline 3, so slots $[1], [2], [3]$.

- $J_1$, profit 20, deadline 2 $\to$ latest free slot $\le 2$ is **slot 2**.
- $J_2$, profit 15, deadline 2 $\to$ slot 2 taken, slot 1 free $\to$ **slot 1**.
- $J_3$, profit 10, deadline 1 $\to$ slot 1 taken, nothing earlier $\to$ **rejected**.
- $J_4$, profit 5, deadline 3 $\to$ **slot 3**.
- $J_5$, profit 1, deadline 3 $\to$ slots 3, 2, 1 all taken $\to$ **rejected**.

Schedule $J_2, J_1, J_4$ in slots 1, 2, 3; **total profit $= 15+20+5 = 40$**.

Note how scheduling $J_1$ at slot 2 rather than slot 1 was what let $J_2$ in. Filling the earliest free slot instead would have put $J_1$ in slot 1, $J_2$ in slot 2, $J_3$ rejected, $J_4$ in slot 3 — the same profit here, but on instances with many tight deadlines the "latest slot" rule strictly dominates.

## Other greedy algorithms, and the classic failure

**Correct and greedy:** Prim's and Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithms (topic 7.10), Dijkstra's shortest path on non-negative weights, fractional knapsack, Huffman, activity selection, optimal merge patterns, and the set-cover approximation.

**Coin change.** To make an amount with the fewest coins, greedy (take the largest coin that fits, repeatedly) is optimal for the Indian and US denominations, and for any **canonical** system, but not in general. With denominations $\{1, 3, 4\}$ and target 6, greedy takes $4 + 1 + 1$ = **3 coins**, while the optimum is $3 + 3$ = **2 coins**. With $\{1, 7, 10\}$ and target 15, greedy gives $10+1+1+1+1+1$ = 6 coins against the optimal $7+7+1$ = 3. Testing whether a given system is canonical is itself a non-trivial problem, so the safe general algorithm is dynamic programming.

**Graph colouring, vertex cover, TSP, bin packing, set cover:** greedy gives a fast approximation with a provable ratio but never the optimum in general. First-fit decreasing for bin packing uses at most $\tfrac{11}{9}\text{OPT} + \tfrac69$ bins; the greedy set-cover is a $\ln n$-approximation and that is essentially the best possible unless P = NP.

blocks.q: For the 0/1 knapsack instance with capacity 8 and items $(w,v)$ = (2,3), (3,4), (4,5), (5,6), the greedy-by-density solution and the optimal solution have values
blocks.exp: Densities are 1.50, 1.33, 1.25, 1.20, so greedy takes items 1 and 2 (weight 5, value 7) and then neither item 3 (needs 4) nor item 4 (needs 5) fits in the remaining 3 units. The optimum takes items 2 and 4: weight $3+5=8$ exactly, value $4+6=10$. This is the standard demonstration that the greedy-choice property fails for 0/1 knapsack.

blocks.q: Six symbols have frequencies 5, 9, 12, 13, 16, 45. The total length of the Huffman-encoded message is
blocks.exp: Merging the two smallest repeatedly produces internal nodes of value 14, 25, 30, 55 and 100, and the total encoded length equals the sum of the internal node values: $14+25+30+55+100 = 224$. The fixed-length alternative would need $\lceil\log_2 6\rceil = 3$ bits per symbol, i.e. 300 bits.

blocks.q: Which greedy rule solves the activity-selection problem optimally?
opts: Choose the activity with the earliest start time
Choose the activity of shortest duration
Choose the activity with the earliest finish time
Choose the activity overlapping the fewest others
blocks.exp: Earliest finish time is the only one of the four that is provably optimal, because finishing soonest maximises the time left for the remaining activities. Earliest start fails on a single all-day activity; shortest duration fails when a short activity straddles the gap between two compatible long ones; fewest-conflicts is intuitive but has counterexamples.

tricks.title: Huffman total = sum of the internal node values
tricks.body: Never compute $\sum f_i d_i$ by reading depths off a drawn tree. Every merge you perform produces one internal node; add those numbers up. For 5, 9, 12, 13, 16, 45 the merges are 14, 25, 30, 55, 100 and the answer 224 falls out with no tree at all.

tricks.title: Fractional optimum bounds the 0/1 optimum
tricks.body: Run fractional knapsack first: its value is an upper bound on the 0/1 answer, and its integral prefix (all whole items taken before the cut) is a lower bound. If the two coincide, the greedy answer happens to be optimal and you are done.

tricks.title: Job sequencing: fill the latest free slot
tricks.body: Sort by profit descending and place each job as late as its deadline permits. Placing jobs early is the standard mistake and loses profit whenever a later job has a tight deadline. Total slots needed is at most $\max d_i$.

tricks.title: To disprove a greedy rule, build a two-item trap
tricks.body: Almost every 'is this greedy rule correct' question is settled by a three-element counterexample. For knapsack, make one high-density item just big enough to block two medium items. For coin change, use $\{1,3,4\}$ and target 6.

tricks.title: Greedy is $O(n\log n)$ because of the sort
tricks.body: If a question asks for the complexity of a greedy algorithm and the algorithm needs an ordering, the answer is $O(n\log n)$ dominated by the sort — unless the input is already sorted or the ordering comes from a heap that is maintained anyway.

traps.title: Greedy by density is optimal for fractional, never guaranteed for 0/1
traps.body: The two problems differ by one word and by the whole complexity class: fractional knapsack is $O(n\log n)$ and greedy; 0/1 knapsack is NP-complete. An option stating that greedy solves 0/1 knapsack optimally is false even if it works on the particular numbers given.

traps.title: Greedy coin change is not always optimal
traps.body: It is optimal for canonical systems such as $\{1,2,5,10,20,50,100\}$, which is why it feels right. With $\{1,3,4\}$ and target 6 it gives 3 coins instead of 2. The question will usually supply a non-standard denomination set precisely to catch this.

traps.title: Huffman codes are not unique but their length is
traps.body: Two different codeword assignments can both be optimal, so 'the Huffman code for this input is ...' may have several right answers, while 'the average code length is ...' has exactly one. Match your answer to which is asked.

traps.title: Optimal substructure alone does not license greed
traps.body: 0/1 knapsack, matrix chain multiplication and LCS all have optimal substructure and none of them is solved greedily. The extra requirement is the greedy-choice property — that a locally best choice is contained in some optimal solution.

topics.title: Dynamic Programming
topics.summary: Overlapping subproblems and memoisation, with LCS, matrix chain multiplication and 0/1 knapsack tables filled in completely, plus LIS, edit distance and the standard DP graph algorithms.

blocks.text:
## When to use dynamic programming

Dynamic programming applies when a problem has both:

**Optimal substructure.** An optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems. (Shared with divide and conquer and with greedy.)

**Overlapping subproblems.** The same subproblems recur many times in the recursion tree, so storing each answer once converts exponential work into polynomial work. (This is what distinguishes DP from divide and conquer, whose subproblems are disjoint.)

The canonical illustration is Fibonacci. The recursion $F(n) = F(n-1)+F(n-2)$ makes $\Theta(\phi^n)$ calls because $F(n-2)$ is recomputed from both branches, and $F(n-3)$ from three places, and so on. Storing each $F(k)$ the first time it is computed reduces this to $\Theta(n)$ — the same recursion, with a table.

**Two implementations, same complexity:**

- **Memoisation (top-down).** Write the natural recursion, but check a table before recursing and store the result before returning. Only the subproblems actually needed get computed, which helps when the table is sparse; the cost is recursion overhead and stack depth.
- **Tabulation (bottom-up).** Fill the table in an order that guarantees every dependency is already present, usually with nested loops. No recursion, better constants, and it permits **space optimisation**: if row $i$ depends only on row $i-1$, keep two rows instead of $n$.

Writing the recurrence correctly is the whole task. The three things to fix, in order, are: what the state is (the table's indices), what the recurrence is, and what the base cases are. Then the running time is (number of states) $\times$ (work per state).

## Longest common subsequence

A **subsequence** need not be contiguous; a **substring** must be. LCS is about subsequences.

For $X = x_1\ldots x_m$ and $Y = y_1 \ldots y_n$, let $c[i][j]$ be the LCS length of the prefixes $X_i$ and $Y_j$:

$$c[i][j] = \begin{cases} 0 & i = 0 \text{ or } j = 0\\ c[i-1][j-1] + 1 & x_i = y_j\\ \max\big(c[i-1][j],\ c[i][j-1]\big) & x_i \ne y_j \end{cases}$$

There are $mn$ states and $O(1)$ work each, so the running time is $\Theta(mn)$ and the space $\Theta(mn)$ — reducible to $\Theta(\min(m,n))$ if only the length is required, but the full table is needed to reconstruct the sequence itself.

**Reconstruction:** start at $c[m][n]$; if $x_i = y_j$ output $x_i$ and move diagonally; otherwise move to whichever of $c[i-1][j]$, $c[i][j-1]$ is larger (either, if equal — which is why several distinct LCSs of the same length may exist).

Related results worth knowing: the LCS of a sequence with its own reverse is the **longest palindromic subsequence**; the **shortest common supersequence** has length $m+n-\text{LCS}$; and the minimum number of insertions and deletions to turn $X$ into $Y$ is $(m - \text{LCS}) + (n - \text{LCS})$.

blocks.text:
## Matrix chain multiplication

Multiplying a $p \times q$ matrix by a $q \times r$ matrix costs $pqr$ scalar multiplications. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the *result* does not depend on the parenthesisation, but the *cost* does — often by orders of magnitude. Given dimensions $p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_n$ for matrices $A_i$ of size $p_{i-1} \times p_i$, find the cheapest parenthesisation.

$$m[i][j] = \begin{cases} 0 & i = j\\[4pt] \displaystyle\min_{i \le k < j}\Big( m[i][k] + m[k+1][j] + p_{i-1}p_k p_j \Big) & i < j\end{cases}$$

There are $\Theta(n^2)$ states and $O(n)$ choices of $k$ each, so the algorithm is $\Theta(n^3)$ time and $\Theta(n^2)$ space. The number of possible parenthesisations of $n$ matrices is the Catalan number $C_{n-1}$, which is exponential — 4862 for $n = 10$ — so exhaustive search is hopeless and DP is essential.

Fill the table by **increasing chain length** $l = j - i + 1$, because $m[i][j]$ depends on strictly shorter chains. Keep a second table $s[i][j]$ recording the minimising $k$, and read the parenthesisation off it recursively.

blocks.text:
## 0/1 knapsack

Items $1\ldots n$ with weights $w_i$ and values $v_i$, capacity $W$. Let $K[i][c]$ be the best value using only the first $i$ items with capacity $c$:

$$K[i][c] = \begin{cases} 0 & i = 0 \text{ or } c = 0\\ K[i-1][c] & w_i > c\\ \max\big(K[i-1][c],\ v_i + K[i-1][c - w_i]\big) & w_i \le c\end{cases}$$

The answer is $K[n][W]$; the table has $(n+1)(W+1)$ entries and each costs $O(1)$, so the algorithm is $\Theta(nW)$.

**$\Theta(nW)$ is pseudo-polynomial, not polynomial.** The input size is $\Theta(n\log W)$ bits, because $W$ is written in binary; $W$ itself is exponential in the number of bits used to write it. So for $W = 2^{64}$ the algorithm is useless even though "$nW$" looks tame. This is exactly why 0/1 knapsack remains NP-complete despite having this algorithm — the distinction is worth a mark on its own.

Space can be reduced to $\Theta(W)$ by keeping one row and iterating the capacity **downwards**, so that each item is used at most once. Iterating upwards instead solves the **unbounded knapsack** problem, where each item may be taken repeatedly — a one-character difference between two different problems.

To recover **which items** were chosen, walk back from $K[n][W]$: if $K[i][c] \ne K[i-1][c]$ then item $i$ was taken, so subtract $w_i$ from $c$ and move to row $i-1$; otherwise just move up.
