blocks.text:
## The rest of the standard DP repertoire

| Problem | State | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fibonacci / climbing stairs | $i$ | $\Theta(n)$ | space $\Theta(1)$ |
| Rod cutting | length $i$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ | unbounded-knapsack shaped |
| Coin change (min coins) | amount $a$ | $\Theta(nA)$ | the correct method when greedy fails |
| Coin change (count ways) | (coin, amount) | $\Theta(nA)$ | loop coins outside to avoid counting permutations |
| Subset sum | (item, sum) | $\Theta(nS)$ | pseudo-polynomial, NP-complete |
| LIS | $i$ | $\Theta(n^2)$, or $\Theta(n\log n)$ with patience sorting | the $n\log n$ version uses binary search over tail values |
| Edit distance (Levenshtein) | $(i,j)$ | $\Theta(mn)$ | $\min$ of insert, delete, replace |
| Optimal BST | $(i,j)$ | $\Theta(n^3)$ | $\Theta(n^2)$ with Knuth's optimisation |
| Matrix chain | $(i,j)$ | $\Theta(n^3)$ | |
| Travelling salesman (Held–Karp) | (subset, last city) | $\Theta(n^2 2^n)$ | still exponential, but far better than $n!$ |
| Floyd–Warshall | $(i,j,k)$ | $\Theta(V^3)$ | all-pairs shortest paths |
| Bellman–Ford | (vertex, edge count) | $\Theta(VE)$ | single source with negative edges |

**Edit distance** deserves its recurrence spelled out, since it is asked as often as LCS:

$$d[i][j] = \begin{cases} j & i = 0\\ i & j = 0\\ d[i-1][j-1] & x_i = y_j\\ 1 + \min\big(d[i-1][j],\ d[i][j-1],\ d[i-1][j-1]\big) & x_i \ne y_j\end{cases}$$

where the three terms are delete, insert and replace respectively.

**Longest increasing subsequence** in $\Theta(n^2)$: $L[i] = 1 + \max\{L[j] : j < i,\ A[j] < A[i]\}$, answer $\max_i L[i]$. The $\Theta(n\log n)$ version maintains an array `tails` where `tails[k]` is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length $k+1$; for each element, binary search for the first tail $\ge$ it and overwrite. The length of `tails` at the end is the answer — but its contents are **not** an LIS, a point questions like to probe.

blocks.q: For matrices $A_1(5\times4)$, $A_2(4\times6)$, $A_3(6\times2)$, $A_4(2\times7)$, the minimum number of scalar multiplications is
blocks.exp: Filling the DP table gives $m[1][2]=120$, $m[2][3]=48$, $m[3][4]=84$, then $m[1][3]=88$ and $m[2][4]=104$, and finally $m[1][4]=\min(244, 414, 158) = 158$ at $k=3$. The optimal order is $(A_1(A_2A_3))A_4$: $48 + 40 + 70 = 158$. Option 3 is the cost of $(A_1A_2)(A_3A_4)$, the worst split.

blocks.q: Why is the $\Theta(nW)$ dynamic program for 0/1 knapsack not a polynomial-time algorithm?
opts: Because $W$ is exponential in the number of bits used to encode it
Because the table cannot be built in $\Theta(nW)$ time
Because the recurrence has exponentially many states
blocks.exp: Polynomial time means polynomial in the *length of the encoded input*, which is $\Theta(n\log W)$ bits. A capacity written with $b$ bits has value up to $2^b$, so $nW$ is exponential in $b$. An algorithm polynomial in the numeric value of an input rather than its encoding length is called pseudo-polynomial, and 0/1 knapsack remains NP-complete because of it.

blocks.q: In the space-optimised 0/1 knapsack using a single array $K[0..W]$, in which direction must the capacity loop run, and why?
opts: Increasing, so each item can be reused
Decreasing, so each item is used at most once
Either direction gives the same result
Increasing, to keep the array sorted
blocks.exp: Processing capacities downwards means $K[c-w_i]$ still holds the value from the previous item's row when it is read, so item $i$ contributes once. Running the loop upwards would read a cell already updated with item $i$, letting the item be taken repeatedly — which is exactly the unbounded-knapsack algorithm, a different problem.

tricks.title: Count states times work to get the complexity
tricks.body: LCS: $mn$ states, $O(1)$ each, so $\Theta(mn)$. Matrix chain: $\Theta(n^2)$ states, $O(n)$ each, so $\Theta(n^3)$. Knapsack: $nW$ states, $O(1)$ each. You never need to analyse the loops — just count the table and the work per cell.

tricks.title: Fill the matrix-chain table by chain length, along diagonals
tricks.body: $m[i][j]$ needs shorter chains only, so sweep $l = 2, 3, \ldots, n$ and within each $l$ take $i = 1 \ldots n-l+1$. Filling row by row reads cells that do not exist yet, which is the usual cause of a wrong table.

tricks.title: $p_{i-1}p_k p_j$ is the cost of the final multiplication
tricks.body: In matrix chain, the third term is always outer-left-dimension $\times$ split-dimension $\times$ outer-right-dimension. Write the dimension vector above the table and read the three subscripts off it rather than re-deriving them.

tricks.title: Knapsack traceback: compare with the cell directly above
tricks.body: Item $i$ is in the solution exactly when $K[i][c] \ne K[i-1][c]$. This makes 'which items were selected' a two-second walk up the last column rather than a re-solve.

tricks.title: Shortest common supersequence $= m + n - \text{LCS}$
tricks.body: Several LCS-family questions are one subtraction away from the table you already built: minimum insertions plus deletions to convert $X$ to $Y$ is $(m-L)+(n-L)$, and the longest palindromic subsequence of $S$ is $\mathrm{LCS}(S, \text{reverse}(S))$.

traps.title: Subsequence is not substring
traps.body: LCS allows gaps; longest common **substring** requires contiguity and has a different recurrence ($c[i][j] = c[i-1][j-1]+1$ on a match, **0** on a mismatch, answer = max over the table). Questions swap the words deliberately.

traps.title: Pseudo-polynomial is not polynomial
traps.body: $\Theta(nW)$ for knapsack and $\Theta(nS)$ for subset sum look polynomial but are exponential in the input length. Any option claiming these DPs prove P = NP, or that knapsack is in P, is wrong.

traps.title: Greedy does not become DP by adding a table
traps.body: DP considers every choice at each state and takes the best; greedy commits to one. If a described algorithm sorts and then makes one pass, it is greedy no matter how much bookkeeping it carries.

traps.title: Memoisation and tabulation have the same complexity
traps.body: Top-down and bottom-up differ in constants, stack usage and which states get computed — never in asymptotic time for the same recurrence. An option claiming memoisation is asymptotically slower because of recursion is wrong.

topics.title: Backtracking and Branch and Bound
topics.summary: State-space trees, bounding functions, N-queens and sum-of-subsets, and the three branch-and-bound search strategies with a reduced-cost-matrix TSP worked in full.

blocks.text:
## The state-space tree

Both techniques search a **state-space tree**: a tree whose root is the empty partial solution, whose edges are decisions, and whose leaves are complete candidate solutions. Exhaustive search visits the whole tree. Backtracking and branch and bound visit only part of it, by **pruning** subtrees that cannot contain what we are looking for.

Vocabulary that questions use precisely:

- **Explicit constraints** restrict what values a component may take (e.g. $x_i \in \{0,1\}$) and define the tree's shape.
- **Implicit constraints** describe how components must relate (e.g. no two queens on a diagonal) and determine which nodes are pruned.
- A **live node** has been generated but not yet fully explored. The **E-node** (expanding node) is the live node currently being expanded. A **dead node** is pruned or fully expanded.
- A **bounding function** decides whether a node can be killed.

**Backtracking** is depth-first: expand the E-node to one child, make that child the new E-node, and go deeper; if a node fails the feasibility test, abandon it and back up to the parent's next child. It is used for problems where we want **any** feasible solution or **all** feasible solutions, and it keeps only the current root-to-node path in memory, so its space is $O(\text{depth})$.

**Branch and bound** is for **optimisation**. Every node carries a bound on the best objective value achievable in its subtree; a node is killed whenever its bound is no better than the best complete solution found so far (the **incumbent**). Because it must compare bounds across the frontier, it keeps *all* live nodes, so its space can be exponential.

| | Backtracking | Branch and bound |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | feasibility — find one or all solutions | optimisation — find the best |
| Traversal | depth-first only | FIFO (BFS), LIFO (D-search), or least-cost | 
| Pruning test | feasibility (constraints violated) | bounding function vs incumbent |
| Live nodes kept | the current path | the whole frontier |
| Typical space | $O(n)$ | $O(2^n)$ in the worst case |
| Typical problems | N-queens, graph colouring, Hamiltonian cycle, sum of subsets | 0/1 knapsack, TSP, job assignment |

Neither technique improves the **worst-case** complexity. N-queens by backtracking is still exponential; TSP by branch and bound is still $O(n^2 2^n)$ or worse. They improve the average case, often dramatically, and that distinction is a frequent exam statement.

## Classic backtracking problems

**N-queens.** Place $n$ queens on an $n\times n$ board with none attacking another. Represent a placement as a vector $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ where $x_i$ is the column of the queen in row $i$ — this bakes in "one queen per row" and reduces the search space from $\binom{n^2}{n}$ to $n^n$, and the column constraint reduces it further to $n!$. Two queens at $(i, x_i)$ and $(j, x_j)$ attack each other iff

$$x_i = x_j \quad\text{or}\quad |i - j| = |x_i - x_j|$$

the second condition covering both diagonals. Counts worth knowing: **4-queens has 2 solutions; 8-queens has 92 solutions, or 12 up to rotation and reflection**; no solution exists for $n = 2$ or $n = 3$.

**Sum of subsets.** Given $n$ positive numbers and a target $M$, find subsets summing to $M$. Sort ascending and use two bounding tests at a node with current sum $s$ and remaining elements $w_{k}\ldots w_n$: prune if $s + w_k > M$ (the next element already overshoots) and prune if $s + \sum_{i=k}^{n} w_i < M$ (even taking everything left falls short). Those two tests are what makes the method beat $2^n$ enumeration in practice.

**Graph $m$-colouring.** Assign one of $m$ colours to each vertex with no two adjacent vertices alike. The state-space tree has branching factor $m$ and depth $V$, so $m^V$ nodes in the worst case. Deciding 3-colourability is NP-complete; 2-colourability is just a BFS bipartiteness test in $O(V+E)$.

**Hamiltonian cycle.** Extend a path vertex by vertex, checking at each step that the next vertex is adjacent to the last and not already used, and that the final vertex is adjacent to the start.

**Knapsack by backtracking** is possible but wasteful, because it must enumerate feasible sets without knowing when to stop — this is precisely the problem branch and bound fixes with a bound.

## Branch and bound: bounds and search orders

A bound must be **optimistic**: for a minimisation problem it must never exceed the true best value in the subtree, so that killing a node whose bound is worse than the incumbent is safe. A tighter bound prunes more but costs more to compute, and the whole art is in that trade-off.

**Search orders.**

- **FIFO branch and bound** takes live nodes from a queue — a breadth-first exploration.
- **LIFO branch and bound** (also called D-search) takes them from a stack — depth-first, so it finds a complete solution quickly and gets an incumbent to prune with early.
- **LC (least cost) branch and bound** always expands the live node with the most promising bound, using a priority queue. It explores the fewest nodes in principle, but keeps the largest frontier and can thrash on memory.

**0/1 knapsack by LCBB.** Convert to minimisation by negating values. At a node where some items are decided, the bound is the value of the decided items plus the **fractional** knapsack solution on the remaining items and remaining capacity — the fractional relaxation is always at least as good as the integral one, so it is a valid optimistic bound. This is the standard illustration that the greedy algorithm of topic 7.7, useless as an exact method, is exactly the right bounding function.

**TSP by LCBB with reduced cost matrices.** A matrix is **reduced** when every row and every column contains at least one zero. Subtracting the row minimum from each row and then the column minimum from each column produces a reduced matrix, and the **total amount subtracted is a lower bound on every tour**, because every tour must use exactly one entry from each row and one from each column. Selecting an edge $i \to j$ adds $\text{(current bound)} + \text{(reduced cost of } i\to j) + \text{(cost of re-reducing after blocking row } i$, column $j$ and the return edge $j\to i$).

blocks.title: Worked example — TSP by least-cost branch and bound
blocks.text:
Four cities with the symmetric cost matrix ($\infty$ on the diagonal):

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | $\infty$ | 10 | 15 | 20 |
| **2** | 10 | $\infty$ | 35 | 25 |
| **3** | 15 | 35 | $\infty$ | 30 |
| **4** | 20 | 25 | 30 | $\infty$ |

**Step 1 — reduce the matrix.**

Row minima are 10, 10, 15, 20, totalling **55**. Subtracting them:

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | $\infty$ | 0 | 5 | 10 |
| **2** | 0 | $\infty$ | 25 | 15 |
| **3** | 0 | 20 | $\infty$ | 15 |
| **4** | 0 | 5 | 10 | $\infty$ |

Column minima are now 0, 0, 5, 10, totalling **15**. Subtracting those gives the reduced matrix $R$:

| $R$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | $\infty$ | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **2** | 0 | $\infty$ | 20 | 5 |
| **3** | 0 | 20 | $\infty$ | 5 |
| **4** | 0 | 5 | 5 | $\infty$ |

Every row and every column now contains a zero. Total reduction $= 55 + 15 = 70$, so the **root bound is 70**: no tour can cost less than 70.

**Step 2 — branch on the first edge out of city 1.**

For each child, the new bound is (parent bound) + (reduced cost of the chosen edge) + (cost of re-reducing the matrix after deleting row $i$, deleting column $j$ and setting the return entry to $\infty$).

*Child $1\to2$.* $R[1][2] = 0$. Delete row 1, delete column 2, set $(2,1) = \infty$. The remaining submatrix on rows $\{2,3,4\}$ and columns $\{1,3,4\}$ is

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & 1 & 3 & 4\\\hline 2 & \infty & 20 & 5\\ 3 & 0 & \infty & 5\\ 4 & 0 & 5 & \infty\end{array}$$

Row 2 has minimum 5 (rows 3 and 4 already hold a zero), so **row reduction 5**, making row 2 read $(\infty, 15, 0)$. Column 3 is now $(15, \infty, 5)$ with minimum 5, so **column reduction 5**. Total added $= 10$, and
$$\text{bound}(1\to2) = 70 + 0 + 10 = \mathbf{80}$$

*Child $1\to3$.* $R[1][3] = 0$. Submatrix on rows $\{2,3,4\}$, columns $\{1,2,4\}$ with $(3,1) = \infty$:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & 1 & 2 & 4\\\hline 2 & 0 & \infty & 5\\ 3 & \infty & 20 & 5\\ 4 & 0 & 5 & \infty\end{array}$$

Row 3 needs 5; rows 2 and 4 need nothing (**row reduction 5**). Column 2 then reads $(\infty, 15, 5)$, minimum 5 (**column reduction 5**). Total 10, so
$$\text{bound}(1\to3) = 70 + 0 + 10 = \mathbf{80}$$

*Child $1\to4$.* $R[1][4] = 0$. Submatrix on rows $\{2,3,4\}$, columns $\{1,2,3\}$ with $(4,1) = \infty$:

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & 1 & 2 & 3\\\hline 2 & 0 & \infty & 20\\ 3 & 0 & 20 & \infty\\ 4 & \infty & 5 & 5\end{array}$$

Only row 4 needs reducing, by 5 (**row reduction 5**), after which every column contains a zero (**column reduction 0**). Total 5, so
$$\text{bound}(1\to4) = 70 + 0 + 5 = \mathbf{75}$$

**Step 3 — expand the least-cost live node, $1\to4$ (bound 75).** Its reduced submatrix is

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & 1 & 2 & 3\\\hline 2 & 0 & \infty & 20\\ 3 & 0 & 20 & \infty\\ 4 & \infty & 0 & 0\end{array}$$

- $4\to2$: edge cost 0; deleting row 4 and column 2 and blocking $(2,1)$ leaves row 2 $= (\infty, 20)$ needing a reduction of 20. Bound $= 75 + 0 + 20 = 95$.
- $4\to3$: edge cost 0; symmetrically, row 3 needs 20. Bound $= 75 + 0 + 20 = 95$.

Both children are worse than the two level-1 nodes still waiting at 80. **The most promising node at level 1 was not on the optimal path** — exactly what a greedy algorithm would have got wrong.

**Step 4 — expand $1\to2$ (bound 80).** Its reduced submatrix is

$$\begin{array}{c|ccc} & 1 & 3 & 4\\\hline 2 & \infty & 10 & 0\\ 3 & 0 & \infty & 5\\ 4 & 0 & 0 & \infty\end{array}$$

- $2\to3$: edge cost 10; afterwards row 3 needs a reduction of 5. Bound $= 80 + 10 + 5 = 95$.
- $2\to4$: edge cost 0; the remaining $2\times2$ submatrix on rows $\{3,4\}$, columns $\{1,3\}$ with $(4,1)$ blocked is $\begin{pmatrix}0 & \infty\\ \infty & 0\end{pmatrix}$, already reduced. Bound $= 80 + 0 + 0 = \mathbf{80}$.

**Step 5 — complete and prune.** From $1\to2\to4$ only city 3 is unvisited, so the tour is forced:

$$1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 3 \to 1, \qquad \text{cost} = 10 + 25 + 30 + 15 = \mathbf{80}$$

The incumbent is now 80. Every live node has bound $\ge 80$, so nothing can beat it; the node $1\to3$ at bound 80 yields the same tour traversed backwards ($1\to3\to4\to2\to1 = 15+30+25+10 = 80$), and every other node is at 95.

**Optimal tour: $1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 3 \to 1$, cost 80.** With four cities there are only $(4-1)!/2 = 3$ distinct tours, so we can check exhaustively: $1\text-2\text-3\text-4\text-1 = 10+35+30+20 = 95$, $1\text-3\text-2\text-4\text-1 = 15+35+25+20 = 95$, and $1\text-2\text-4\text-3\text-1 = 80$. Confirmed.

Two lessons to carry away. The root bound of 70 is a genuine lower bound but is **not attained** — bounds are optimistic estimates, not predictions. And branch and bound must retain the whole frontier, because the node that looked best at level 1 (bound 75) led nowhere, while a node at 80 held the optimum.

blocks.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes backtracking from branch and bound?
opts: Backtracking is used for optimisation problems, branch and bound for feasibility problems
Backtracking explores the state-space tree depth-first, while branch and bound may use FIFO, LIFO or least-cost order
Branch and bound always runs in polynomial time
Backtracking requires a bounding function, branch and bound does not
blocks.exp: Backtracking is inherently depth-first and is used to find feasible solutions; branch and bound targets optimisation and may traverse the tree in breadth-first, depth-first or least-cost order according to how live nodes are stored. Neither guarantees polynomial time, and it is branch and bound — not backtracking — that needs a bounding function.

blocks.q: In the reduced-cost-matrix method for TSP, the sum of all row and column reductions at the root represents
opts: the exact cost of the optimal tour
a lower bound on the cost of every tour
an upper bound on the cost of every tour
the cost of the greedy nearest-neighbour tour
blocks.exp: Every tour uses exactly one entry from each row and one from each column, so the amounts subtracted during reduction are paid by every tour without exception. The reduction total is therefore a valid lower bound, and pruning any node whose bound exceeds the incumbent is safe. It is rarely attained — in the worked example the root bound is 70 while the optimum is 80.

blocks.q: How many solutions does the 4-queens problem have, and how many does 8-queens have?
blocks.exp: 4-queens has exactly 2 solutions, which are mirror images of each other. 8-queens has 92 solutions in total, reducing to 12 distinct ones once rotations and reflections are factored out. The figure 12 is the count of *fundamental* solutions, not of all solutions — a distinction options exploit.

tricks.title: Vector representation collapses the search space
tricks.body: For N-queens, representing the board as $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ with $x_i$ = column of the queen in row $i$ turns $\binom{n^2}{n}$ placements into $n^n$, and disallowing repeats makes it $n!$. Any question about 'the size of the state-space tree' depends entirely on which representation is described.

tricks.title: The diagonal test is one line
tricks.body: Queens at rows $i, j$ conflict diagonally exactly when $|i-j| = |x_i - x_j|$. This single equation replaces checking both diagonals separately, and it is what you should apply when a question shows a partial board and asks whether a placement is legal.

tricks.title: The fractional relaxation is the knapsack bound
tricks.body: For 0/1 knapsack by branch and bound, the bound at any node is 'value of the items already fixed plus the fractional-knapsack value of the rest'. Computing it is a greedy pass by density — quick to do by hand under exam conditions.

tricks.title: Reduce rows first, then columns, and add the totals
tricks.body: The root bound for TSP is the sum of all row minima plus the sum of the column minima of the row-reduced matrix. Doing columns first gives the same total, but mixing the order mid-calculation does not — pick one and keep to it.

tricks.title: Sort ascending for sum-of-subsets
tricks.body: With the numbers sorted, the 'overshoot' test $s + w_k > M$ prunes an entire tail at once and the 'undershoot' test uses a running suffix sum you compute once. Unsorted input makes both tests nearly useless.

traps.title: Neither method improves the worst case
traps.body: Backtracking and branch and bound prune, but the pruned tree can still be exponential. Any option saying that branch and bound solves TSP or knapsack in polynomial time is false; the correct statement is that they reduce the *average* number of nodes explored.

traps.title: Branch and bound's memory, not its time, is the usual surprise
traps.body: Backtracking stores only the current path, $O(n)$. LC branch and bound stores the entire live-node frontier, which can be exponential — this is why depth-first (LIFO) branch and bound is preferred in practice despite exploring more nodes.

traps.title: The bound must be optimistic
traps.body: For minimisation the bound must be a *lower* bound (and for maximisation, an upper bound). Using a pessimistic bound prunes nodes that contain the optimum and silently returns a wrong answer — the most common conceptual error in this topic.

traps.title: 12 versus 92 for 8-queens
traps.body: 92 is the number of solutions; 12 is the number of distinct solutions modulo the eight symmetries of the square. Read whether the question says 'distinct', 'fundamental' or 'up to symmetry'.

topics.title: Graph Algorithms
topics.summary: Representations, BFS and DFS with edge classification, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall, Prim and Kruskal, and maximum flow with the min-cut theorem.

blocks.text:
## Representations, and why the choice changes complexities

| | Adjacency matrix | Adjacency list |
|---|---|---|
| Space | $\Theta(V^2)$ | $\Theta(V+E)$ |
| Is $(u,v)$ an edge? | $\Theta(1)$ | $\Theta(\deg u)$ |
| List all neighbours of $u$ | $\Theta(V)$ | $\Theta(\deg u)$ |
| Add an edge | $\Theta(1)$ | $\Theta(1)$ |
| BFS / DFS | $\Theta(V^2)$ | $\Theta(V+E)$ |
| Best for | dense graphs, edge queries | sparse graphs, traversal |

A graph is **dense** when $E = \Theta(V^2)$ and **sparse** when $E = O(V)$. Since almost every stated complexity in this topic assumes adjacency lists, a question that specifies a matrix is usually testing whether you notice that traversal becomes $\Theta(V^2)$.

Counting facts: an undirected simple graph on $V$ vertices has at most $\binom{V}{2} = V(V-1)/2$ edges; a directed one has at most $V(V-1)$. A tree on $V$ vertices has exactly $V-1$ edges. A connected graph needs at least $V-1$ edges; a graph with more than $\binom{V-1}{2}$ edges is necessarily connected. The sum of all degrees is $2E$ (handshaking lemma).

## BFS and DFS

**BFS** explores by distance: put the source in a queue, and repeatedly dequeue a vertex and enqueue its undiscovered neighbours. It runs in $\Theta(V+E)$ and yields:

- **Shortest paths in an unweighted graph** (or one with all weights equal), because vertices leave the queue in non-decreasing order of distance.
- A **BFS tree** whose root-to-$v$ path is a shortest path.
- A **bipartiteness test**: two-colour by level; the graph is bipartite iff no edge joins two vertices of the same level, equivalently iff it has no odd cycle.
- The **connected components** of an undirected graph, by restarting from each unvisited vertex.

**DFS** explores by depth, recursively or with an explicit stack, also in $\Theta(V+E)$. Recording a discovery time $d[v]$ and a finish time $f[v]$ for every vertex classifies each edge $(u,v)$:

| Edge type | Condition | Occurs in |
|---|---|---|
| **Tree** | $v$ is undiscovered when $(u,v)$ is explored | both |
| **Back** | $v$ is an ancestor of $u$ (grey when reached) | both |
| **Forward** | $v$ is a descendant reached again, $d[u] < d[v]$ | directed only |
| **Cross** | all other cases | directed only |

In an **undirected** graph DFS produces only tree and back edges — a fact worth stating, because it is the basis for cycle detection.

**Cycle detection.** A directed graph has a cycle iff DFS finds a **back edge**. An undirected graph has a cycle iff DFS finds a back edge to a vertex other than the immediate parent, or equivalently iff $E \ge V$ in a connected graph, or iff a union-find pass ever unions two vertices already in the same set.

**Topological sort** orders a DAG so every edge points forwards. Two methods: run DFS and output vertices in **decreasing order of finish time**; or run **Kahn's algorithm**, repeatedly removing a vertex of in-degree 0. Both are $\Theta(V+E)$. A topological order exists iff the graph is acyclic, and it is unique iff at every step exactly one vertex has in-degree 0 (equivalently, the order forms a Hamiltonian path in the DAG).

**Strongly connected components** of a directed graph, by **Kosaraju**: DFS the graph pushing vertices onto a stack by finish time; reverse every edge; DFS the reversed graph popping from the stack, each tree being one SCC. Two passes, $\Theta(V+E)$. **Tarjan's** algorithm does it in one pass with low-link values. Condensing each SCC to a single vertex always yields a DAG.

**Articulation points and bridges** use DFS low-link values: the root is an articulation point iff it has $\ge 2$ DFS children; a non-root $u$ is one iff some child $v$ has $\text{low}[v] \ge d[u]$. An edge $(u,v)$ is a **bridge** iff $\text{low}[v] > d[u]$. Both are $\Theta(V+E)$.

## Shortest paths

| Algorithm | Handles | Time | Technique |
|---|---|---|---|
| BFS | unweighted | $\Theta(V+E)$ | traversal |
| **Dijkstra** (binary heap) | non-negative weights, single source | $O((V+E)\log V)$ | greedy |
| Dijkstra (array) | as above | $\Theta(V^2)$ — better when dense | greedy |
| Dijkstra (Fibonacci heap) | as above | $O(E + V\log V)$ | greedy |
| **Bellman–Ford** | negative weights, single source, detects negative cycles | $\Theta(VE)$ | dynamic programming |
| DAG shortest path | any weights, must be acyclic | $\Theta(V+E)$ | topological order + relax |
| **Floyd–Warshall** | negative weights, all pairs | $\Theta(V^3)$ | dynamic programming |
| Johnson | sparse, negative weights, all pairs | $O(V^2\log V + VE)$ | reweighting + Dijkstra |

**Dijkstra** maintains a set of finalised vertices and repeatedly finalises the unfinalised vertex of smallest tentative distance, then relaxes its outgoing edges. **It is greedy, and it is correct only for non-negative weights**, because it assumes a finalised distance can never be improved later — an assumption a negative edge destroys. A three-vertex counterexample: $s\to a = 2$, $s\to b = 3$, $b\to a = -2$. Dijkstra finalises $a$ at distance 2, then finalises $b$ at 3, and never reconsiders $a$ — whose true shortest distance is $3 + (-2) = 1$ via $b$. Note that reweighting by adding a constant to every edge does **not** fix this, because it penalises paths with more edges.

**Bellman–Ford** relaxes **every edge** $V-1$ times. After $k$ passes the distances are correct for all shortest paths using at most $k$ edges, and since a simple shortest path has at most $V-1$ edges, $V-1$ passes suffice. Running one extra, $V$-th pass and finding any edge still relaxable proves a **negative-weight cycle reachable from the source**. Early termination when a pass changes nothing is the standard optimisation.

**Floyd–Warshall** is three nested loops over a distance matrix:

$$d^{(k)}[i][j] = \min\Big(d^{(k-1)}[i][j],\ d^{(k-1)}[i][k] + d^{(k-1)}[k][j]\Big)$$

where $k$ ranges over the allowed **intermediate** vertices. The loop order matters absolutely: $k$ must be the **outermost** loop. Negative edges are fine; a negative cycle shows up as a negative entry on the diagonal. Adding a predecessor matrix recovers the paths themselves.

blocks.title: Worked example — Dijkstra, Floyd–Warshall and both MST algorithms on one graph
blocks.text:
Undirected weighted graph on $\{A,B,C,D,E,F\}$:

| Edge | Weight | | Edge | Weight |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A–B | 4 | | C–E | 10 |
| A–C | 2 | | D–E | 2 |
| B–C | 1 | | D–F | 6 |
| B–D | 5 | | E–F | 3 |
| C–D | 8 | | | |

**(a) Dijkstra from $A$.**

| Step | Finalised | dist A | B | C | D | E | F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| init | — | 0 | $\infty$ | $\infty$ | $\infty$ | $\infty$ | $\infty$ |
| 1 | **A** (0) | 0 | 4 | 2 | $\infty$ | $\infty$ | $\infty$ |
| 2 | **C** (2) | 0 | **3** | 2 | 10 | 12 | $\infty$ |
| 3 | **B** (3) | 0 | 3 | 2 | **8** | 12 | $\infty$ |
| 4 | **D** (8) | 0 | 3 | 2 | 8 | **10** | 14 |
| 5 | **E** (10) | 0 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 10 | **13** |
| 6 | **F** (13) | 0 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 10 | 13 |

Two relaxations are worth pointing at. At step 2, $B$ drops from 4 to 3 because $A\to C\to B$ costs $2+1 = 3$ — the direct edge is not the shortest path. At step 3, $D$ drops from 10 to 8 via $A\to C\to B\to D = 2+1+5$. At step 5, $F$ drops from 14 to 13 via $E$.

**Final distances: $A{=}0$, $C{=}2$, $B{=}3$, $D{=}8$, $E{=}10$, $F{=}13$.**

**(b) Floyd–Warshall on a small directed graph.** Take vertices $1,2,3,4$ with edges $1\to2 = 5$, $1\to4 = 10$, $2\to3 = 3$, $3\to4 = 1$, and $\infty$ elsewhere.

*After $k=1$:* nothing changes — no edge enters vertex 1, so it is never an intermediate.

*After $k=2$:* $d[1][3] = \min(\infty,\ d[1][2] + d[2][3]) = \min(\infty, 5+3) = \mathbf{8}$.

*After $k=3$:* $d[1][4] = \min(10,\ d[1][3] + d[3][4]) = \min(10, 8+1) = \mathbf{9}$, and $d[2][4] = \min(\infty,\ d[2][3]+d[3][4]) = \min(\infty, 3+1) = \mathbf{4}$.

*After $k=4$:* nothing, since no edge leaves vertex 4.

Final matrix (rows = source):

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | 0 | 5 | 8 | **9** |
| **2** | $\infty$ | 0 | 3 | 4 |
| **3** | $\infty$ | $\infty$ | 0 | 1 |
| **4** | $\infty$ | $\infty$ | $\infty$ | 0 |

Note that $d[1][4]$ improved from the direct edge 10 to 9 only at $k=3$, i.e. only once vertex 3 was permitted as an intermediate — which is why running the $k$ loop innermost produces wrong answers.

**(c) Kruskal on the graph of part (a).** Sort the edges: B–C (1), A–C (2), D–E (2), E–F (3), A–B (4), B–D (5), D–F (6), C–D (8), C–E (10).

| Edge | Weight | Accept? | Components after |
|---|---|---|---|
| B–C | 1 | yes | {B,C} |
| A–C | 2 | yes | {A,B,C} |
| D–E | 2 | yes | {A,B,C}, {D,E} |
| E–F | 3 | yes | {A,B,C}, {D,E,F} |
| A–B | 4 | **no** — cycle | unchanged |
| B–D | 5 | yes | all six joined |

Five edges accepted, as required ($V-1 = 5$). **MST weight $= 1+2+2+3+5 = 13$.**

**(d) Prim from $A$ on the same graph.**

| Step | Tree set | Cheapest crossing edge | Added |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | {A} | A–C (2) | C |
| 2 | {A,C} | B–C (1) | B |
| 3 | {A,B,C} | B–D (5) — cheaper than C–D (8), C–E (10) | D |
| 4 | {A,B,C,D} | D–E (2) | E |
| 5 | {A,B,C,D,E} | E–F (3) — cheaper than D–F (6) | F |

**MST weight $= 2+1+5+2+3 = 13$**, the same edge set as Kruskal found. The two algorithms always produce the same *weight*; they produce the same *edge set* here because all edge weights happen to be distinct, which makes the MST unique.

blocks.text:
## Minimum spanning trees

An MST is a spanning tree of minimum total weight; it has exactly $V-1$ edges and exists iff the graph is connected.

| | Prim | Kruskal |
|---|---|---|
| Grows | one tree from a start vertex | a forest, merging components |
| Data structure | priority queue of vertices | sorted edge list + union-find |
| Time | $O(E\log V)$ with binary heap, $\Theta(V^2)$ with array, $O(E + V\log V)$ with Fibonacci heap | $O(E\log E) = O(E\log V)$ |
| Better for | **dense** graphs (the $\Theta(V^2)$ array version) | **sparse** graphs |
| Handles disconnected input | no — finds one component's tree | yes — produces a minimum spanning forest |

Both are greedy, and both are justified by the **cut property**: for any partition of the vertices into two non-empty sets, the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut belongs to some MST. Kruskal additionally uses the **cycle property**: the maximum-weight edge of any cycle belongs to no MST (if it is the unique maximum).

Results asked about repeatedly:

- If **all edge weights are distinct**, the MST is **unique**. If weights repeat, several MSTs may exist but all have the same total weight.
- An MST is also a **minimum bottleneck spanning tree**: it minimises the largest edge used. The converse fails — a minimum bottleneck spanning tree need not be an MST.
- Adding a constant $c$ to every edge weight does not change which tree is minimum (every spanning tree gains exactly $(V-1)c$). Multiplying by a positive constant likewise. But this is **not** true for shortest paths, where paths have different edge counts.
- The maximum spanning tree is found by running either algorithm with the comparison reversed.
- A single edge of minimum weight in the whole graph is always in some MST; a single edge of maximum weight may or may not be.

## Maximum flow

A **flow network** is a directed graph with a capacity $c(u,v) \ge 0$ on every edge, a source $s$ and a sink $t$. A **flow** obeys the capacity constraint $0 \le f(u,v) \le c(u,v)$ and conservation at every vertex other than $s$ and $t$. Its **value** is the net flow out of $s$.

**Ford–Fulkerson** repeatedly finds an **augmenting path** from $s$ to $t$ in the **residual graph** — where a forward edge has residual capacity $c - f$ and every used edge gains a backward residual edge of capacity $f$, allowing flow to be *undone* — and pushes the path's bottleneck capacity along it. The backward edges are what make the method correct rather than merely greedy.

- With integer capacities Ford–Fulkerson terminates and runs in $O(E \cdot |f^*|)$, where $|f^*|$ is the maximum flow value. That depends on the *capacities*, so it can be terrible: the classic graph with capacities $10^6, 10^6, 1$ takes $2 \times 10^6$ augmentations if the path through the unit edge is always chosen.
- **Edmonds–Karp** fixes this by choosing the **shortest** augmenting path (BFS), giving $O(VE^2)$ independent of capacities.
- **Dinic's algorithm** uses level graphs and blocking flows for $O(V^2E)$, and $O(E\sqrt V)$ on unit-capacity graphs.

An **$s$–$t$ cut** partitions the vertices into $S \ni s$ and $T \ni t$; its capacity is the sum of capacities of edges from $S$ to $T$ only (edges from $T$ to $S$ are **not** counted).

**Max-flow min-cut theorem.** The maximum flow value equals the minimum cut capacity. Three statements are equivalent: $f$ is a maximum flow; the residual graph contains no augmenting path; $|f| = c(S,T)$ for some cut. To *find* the minimum cut after computing the max flow, let $S$ be the set of vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph; the edges from $S$ to $T$ are all saturated and form the minimum cut.

Applications: **maximum bipartite matching** (add a source to one side and a sink to the other with unit capacities; max flow = maximum matching size), edge-disjoint and vertex-disjoint paths (Menger's theorem), and project selection.

**Integrality theorem.** With integer capacities there is always a maximum flow in which every edge carries an integer flow — which is what makes the matching reduction work.

blocks.title: Worked example — maximum flow and the minimum cut
blocks.text:
Network with source $s$, sink $t$ and internal vertices $v_1, v_2, v_3, v_4$:

$s\to v_1 = 16$, $s \to v_2 = 13$, $v_1 \to v_2 = 10$, $v_2 \to v_1 = 4$, $v_1 \to v_3 = 12$, $v_3 \to v_2 = 9$, $v_2 \to v_4 = 14$, $v_4 \to v_3 = 7$, $v_3 \to t = 20$, $v_4 \to t = 4$.

**Augmentation 1:** $s \to v_1 \to v_3 \to t$. Bottleneck $= \min(16, 12, 20) = \mathbf{12}$. Flow so far 12.

**Augmentation 2:** $s \to v_2 \to v_4 \to t$. Bottleneck $= \min(13, 14, 4) = \mathbf{4}$. Flow so far 16.

**Augmentation 3:** $s \to v_2 \to v_4 \to v_3 \to t$. Residual capacities: $s\to v_2$ has $13-4 = 9$, $v_2 \to v_4$ has $14-4 = 10$, $v_4 \to v_3$ has 7, $v_3 \to t$ has $20 - 12 = 8$. Bottleneck $= \min(9, 10, 7, 8) = \mathbf{7}$. Flow so far 23.

**Is 23 maximum?** Look for another augmenting path in the residual graph. From $s$: $s\to v_1$ still has $16-12 = 4$ residual. From $v_1$: $v_1\to v_3$ is saturated (12/12); $v_1 \to v_2$ has 10 residual, so reach $v_2$. From $v_2$: $v_2 \to v_4$ has $14-11 = 3$ residual, so reach $v_4$. From $v_4$: $v_4 \to t$ is saturated (4/4) and $v_4 \to v_3$ is saturated (7/7). Dead end. Also from $v_2$, the residual edge $v_2 \to v_1$ leads backwards only. **No augmenting path exists, so the maximum flow is 23.**

**Reading off the minimum cut.** The vertices reachable from $s$ in the residual graph are $S = \{s, v_1, v_2, v_4\}$; the rest is $T = \{v_3, t\}$. Edges from $S$ to $T$:

$$v_1 \to v_3\ (12), \qquad v_4 \to v_3\ (7), \qquad v_4 \to t\ (4)$$

$$c(S,T) = 12 + 7 + 4 = \mathbf{23}$$

which equals the flow value, as the max-flow min-cut theorem guarantees. Note that the edge $v_3 \to v_2$ runs from $T$ to $S$ and contributes **nothing** to the cut capacity — counting it would give 32 and is the standard error.

Every edge crossing the minimum cut is saturated, and every edge crossing back carries zero flow. Both conditions hold here: $v_1\to v_3$ carries 12/12, $v_4 \to v_3$ carries 7/7, $v_4\to t$ carries 4/4, and $v_3 \to v_2$ carries 0/9.

blocks.q: Dijkstra's algorithm may give an incorrect answer when the graph contains
blocks.exp: Dijkstra finalises the nearest unfinalised vertex and never reconsiders it, which is only sound if no later path can be shorter — and a negative edge makes exactly that possible. Cycles of non-negative weight are harmless (a shortest path never uses one), and ties or low-degree vertices are irrelevant. Bellman-Ford is the algorithm to use instead.

blocks.q: In the Floyd-Warshall algorithm, why must the loop over the intermediate vertex $k$ be the outermost of the three loops?
opts: Because $d^{(k)}$ must be fully computed from $d^{(k-1)}$ before $k+1$ is allowed as an intermediate
To reduce the space from $\Theta(V^3)$ to $\Theta(V^2)$
blocks.exp: The recurrence defines $d^{(k)}$ in terms of $d^{(k-1)}$, so all pairs must be updated for intermediate set $\{1..k\}$ before moving to $\{1..k+1\}$. Putting $k$ innermost updates some pairs with a larger intermediate set than others and produces wrong distances. The in-place single-matrix implementation is still correct with $k$ outermost, because the row and column $k$ do not change during pass $k$.

blocks.q: A connected undirected graph has all distinct edge weights. Which statement is true?
opts: It has exactly one minimum spanning tree and exactly one shortest path between every pair
It has exactly one minimum spanning tree
It may have several minimum spanning trees of equal weight
Prim and Kruskal may produce spanning trees of different total weight
blocks.exp: Distinct weights force the MST to be unique, by the cut property: for every cut, the minimum crossing edge is strictly smallest and must be in every MST. Shortest paths are a separate matter and can still tie in structure, so option 1 overclaims. Prim and Kruskal always produce the same total weight regardless of ties, so option 4 is false.

tricks.title: Dijkstra with an array is $\Theta(V^2)$ and that is sometimes better
tricks.body: On a dense graph with $E = \Theta(V^2)$, the heap version's $O(E\log V) = O(V^2\log V)$ is worse than the simple array scan's $\Theta(V^2)$. If a question stresses that the graph is dense or given as an adjacency matrix, the intended answer is $\Theta(V^2)$.

tricks.title: Bellman-Ford pass $k$ finishes all $k$-edge paths
tricks.body: After $k$ relaxation passes every vertex reachable by a shortest path of at most $k$ edges has its final distance. This answers 'what are the distances after 2 passes' questions directly, without simulating edge by edge.

tricks.title: Read the minimum cut off the residual graph
tricks.body: After computing a max flow, BFS from $s$ in the residual graph. The reachable set is $S$; the answer is the sum of the **original** capacities of edges from $S$ to $T$ only. Never count edges pointing back into $S$.

tricks.title: Prim for dense, Kruskal for sparse
tricks.body: Kruskal's $O(E\log E)$ is dominated by sorting the edges, so it wins when $E$ is small. Prim's array version is $\Theta(V^2)$ regardless of $E$, so it wins when $E$ approaches $V^2$. If the edges arrive already sorted, Kruskal drops to $O(E\,\alpha(V))$.

tricks.title: Count edges to settle tree questions instantly
tricks.body: A spanning tree has $V-1$ edges; a graph with $V$ vertices and $V$ edges has exactly one cycle; a forest with $c$ components has $V-c$ edges. Many graph questions are answered by this arithmetic alone.

traps.title: Adding a constant to every edge breaks shortest paths
traps.body: It is safe for MST (every spanning tree has $V-1$ edges, so all gain equally) but not for shortest paths, where a 5-edge path gains $5c$ and a 2-edge path only $2c$. This is exactly why you cannot 'fix' negative edges for Dijkstra by shifting them; Johnson's algorithm uses a potential function precisely to shift them without distorting path costs.

traps.title: Cut capacity counts one direction only
traps.body: For an $s$-$t$ cut $(S,T)$, only edges from $S$ to $T$ count. Edges from $T$ back to $S$ contribute nothing. Including them inflates the answer and is the single most common max-flow arithmetic error.

traps.title: Cross and forward edges never appear in undirected DFS
traps.body: An undirected DFS produces only tree and back edges. Options listing forward or cross edges for an undirected graph are wrong regardless of the picture.

traps.title: A minimum bottleneck spanning tree need not be an MST
traps.body: Every MST minimises the maximum edge, so every MST is a minimum bottleneck spanning tree. The reverse implication is false, and questions state it backwards.

topics.title: Complexity Theory: P, NP and NP-completeness
topics.summary: Decision problems and certificates, the four classes and their containments, polynomial-time reduction with the direction stated correctly, and the standard NP-complete list.

blocks.text:
## Decision problems and certificates

Complexity classes are defined over **decision problems** — problems whose answer is yes or no — because a class is formally a set of languages. An optimisation problem such as "find the largest clique" is recast as "does this graph contain a clique of size $\ge k$?" Nothing is lost: given a fast decider, binary search on $k$ finds the optimum with a polynomial number of calls. Questions sometimes ask why complexity theory bothers with decision versions, and this is the answer.

**Class P.** Languages decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in time polynomial in the input length. These are the problems we consider tractable. Members: sorting, shortest path, matching, linear programming, primality testing (AKS, 2002), 2-SAT, Euler circuit, greatest common divisor.

**Class NP.** Two equivalent definitions, and questions use both:

1. Languages decidable by a **non-deterministic** Turing machine in polynomial time. (This is what the N stands for — **not** "non-polynomial".)
2. Languages for which a **yes** instance has a **certificate** (a proposed solution) that a deterministic machine can **verify** in polynomial time.

The second is the useful one. A graph's Hamiltonian cycle can be checked in $O(V)$ once someone hands you the cycle; finding it is the hard part. Note the asymmetry: NP requires short proofs only for **yes** instances. Proving that a graph has *no* Hamiltonian cycle has no known short certificate — that is what **co-NP** is for.

**Class co-NP.** Languages whose **complement** is in NP: a **no** instance has a short verifiable certificate. Tautology checking and "this formula is unsatisfiable" live here.

$$P \subseteq NP, \qquad P \subseteq \text{co-}NP, \qquad P \subseteq NP \cap \text{co-}NP$$

$P \subseteq NP$ because a deterministic machine is a non-deterministic one that never branches; equivalently, if you can solve it quickly you can verify it quickly by ignoring the certificate and solving it. Whether the containment is strict is the P vs NP question, still open.

## Reduction, and the direction everyone reverses

A **polynomial-time (Karp) reduction** from $A$ to $B$, written $A \le_p B$, is a polynomial-time computable function $f$ such that

$$x \in A \iff f(x) \in B$$

Read it as **"$A$ is no harder than $B$"**, because a decider for $B$ plus the transformation $f$ gives a decider for $A$. Two consequences follow immediately and are worth memorising as a pair:

- If $A \le_p B$ and $B \in P$, then $A \in P$. (Easiness flows **backwards** along the arrow.)
- If $A \le_p B$ and $A$ is NP-hard, then $B$ is NP-hard. (Hardness flows **forwards**.)

**Definitions.**

- $B$ is **NP-hard** if $A \le_p B$ for **every** $A \in NP$. NP-hard problems need not be in NP, need not be decision problems, and need not even be decidable.
- $B$ is **NP-complete** if $B$ is NP-hard **and** $B \in NP$. These are the hardest problems *inside* NP.

$$\textbf{NP-complete} = \textbf{NP} \cap \textbf{NP-hard}$$

**The direction students get backwards.** To prove that your problem $X$ is NP-hard, you must reduce a **known** NP-hard problem **to** $X$:

$$\text{3-SAT} \le_p X \qquad \textbf{(correct)}$$

not

$$X \le_p \text{3-SAT} \qquad \textbf{(useless — proves only that } X \text{ is in NP-ish territory, i.e. no harder than 3-SAT)}$$

The memory device: **"reduce from the known-hard problem."** You are showing that solving $X$ would let you solve something already known to be hard, so $X$ inherits the hardness. Reducing $X$ to 3-SAT shows only that $X$ is *at most* as hard as 3-SAT, which every problem in NP already is.

So an NP-completeness proof has exactly two parts, and a question may ask for either:

1. **$X \in NP$** — exhibit a certificate and a polynomial verifier.
2. **$X$ is NP-hard** — pick a known NP-complete problem $K$, construct a polynomial-time map $f$ from instances of $K$ to instances of $X$, and prove the equivalence in **both** directions ($y$ is a yes-instance of $K$ iff $f(y)$ is a yes-instance of $X$).

Reductions are **transitive**: $A \le_p B$ and $B \le_p C$ give $A \le_p C$. That is why only the first NP-completeness proof had to be done from the definition of a Turing machine.

blocks.title: The consequences to state precisely
blocks.text:
- If **any** NP-complete problem is in P, then $P = NP$ — because everything in NP reduces to it.
- If **any** problem in NP is not in P, then $P \ne NP$ and **no** NP-complete problem is in P.
- If an NP-complete problem is in co-NP, then $NP = \text{co-}NP$.
- If $P = NP$ then $NP = \text{co-}NP$. The converse is not known.
- **Ladner's theorem:** if $P \ne NP$, there exist problems in $NP \setminus P$ that are not NP-complete — the **NP-intermediate** class. Graph isomorphism and integer factoring are the standard candidates; neither is known to be NP-complete and neither is known to be in P.
- NP-hard problems can be **undecidable**. The halting problem is NP-hard (everything in NP reduces to it) but **not** NP-complete, because it is not in NP — no finite certificate proves that a machine never halts.
- $P \subseteq NP \subseteq PSPACE \subseteq EXPTIME$, and $P \subsetneq EXPTIME$ is known by the time hierarchy theorem — so at least one of those containments is strict, though we cannot say which.

## The standard NP-complete problems

**Cook–Levin theorem (1971):** SAT — deciding whether a Boolean formula in CNF is satisfiable — is NP-complete. It was proved directly, by encoding the computation of an arbitrary polynomial-time non-deterministic Turing machine as a formula. Every later proof reduces from SAT or its descendants.

The usual reduction chain:

$$\text{SAT} \to \text{3-SAT} \to \begin{cases}\text{CLIQUE} \to \text{VERTEX COVER} \to \text{HAMILTONIAN CYCLE} \to \text{TSP}\\ \text{3-COLOURING}\\ \text{SUBSET SUM} \to \text{PARTITION} \to \text{KNAPSACK, BIN PACKING}\end{cases}$$

**Complementary pairs.** $S$ is an independent set of $G$ iff $V \setminus S$ is a vertex cover iff $S$ is a clique in the complement graph $\bar G$. So a maximum clique of size $k$ corresponds to a minimum vertex cover of size $V - k$, and the three problems reduce to each other in linear time.

**The easy/hard boundary — the single richest source of exam items.**

| In P | NP-complete |
|---|---|
| 2-SAT | 3-SAT |
| Horn-SAT | CNF-SAT |
| 2-colouring (bipartiteness) | 3-colouring |
| Euler circuit / path | Hamiltonian circuit / path |
| Shortest simple path | **Longest** simple path |
| Minimum spanning tree | Steiner tree, degree-bounded spanning tree |
| Matching in general graphs | 3-dimensional matching |
| Linear programming | Integer linear programming |
| Primality testing | Integer factoring (NP-intermediate candidate, not known NP-complete) |
| Fractional knapsack | 0/1 knapsack |
| Minimum cut | Maximum cut |

**Pseudo-polynomial algorithms and weak NP-completeness.** 0/1 knapsack has an $O(nW)$ dynamic program and subset sum an $O(nS)$ one, yet both are NP-complete. The resolution is that $W$ and $S$ are written in binary, so they are exponential in the input length. Problems that remain NP-complete even when the numbers are written in unary are called **strongly** NP-complete (3-SAT, TSP, graph colouring); those that become polynomial under unary encoding are **weakly** NP-complete (knapsack, subset sum, partition). Strongly NP-complete problems admit no pseudo-polynomial algorithm unless P = NP.

**Approximation.** Since exact solutions are out of reach, we bound the ratio to the optimum. Vertex cover has a simple 2-approximation (take both endpoints of a maximal matching). Metric TSP has a 2-approximation from an MST and a 1.5-approximation from Christofides' algorithm. **General TSP has no constant-factor polynomial approximation unless P = NP**, which is proved by a reduction from Hamiltonian cycle. Set cover has a $\ln n$-approximation and no better unless P = NP.

blocks.title: Worked example — proving a problem NP-complete, in the right direction
blocks.text:
**Problem.** DOUBLE-CLIQUE: given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, does $G$ contain two vertex-disjoint cliques each of size $k$?

**Part 1: DOUBLE-CLIQUE $\in$ NP.** The certificate is the two vertex sets $S_1, S_2$. The verifier checks $|S_1| = |S_2| = k$, that $S_1 \cap S_2 = \varnothing$, and that every pair within each set is joined by an edge. That is $O(k^2)$ edge lookups, polynomial in the input size. Done.

**Part 2: DOUBLE-CLIQUE is NP-hard.** Reduce **from** the known NP-complete CLIQUE. (Reducing DOUBLE-CLIQUE to CLIQUE would prove nothing about its hardness.)

Given an instance $(G, k)$ of CLIQUE, construct $f(G,k) = (G', k)$ where $G'$ is $G$ together with a disjoint copy of a complete graph $K_k$ on $k$ fresh vertices, with no edges between the two parts. Building $G'$ takes time $O(|G| + k^2)$ — polynomial.

*If $G$ has a clique of size $k$:* that clique and the added $K_k$ are two vertex-disjoint cliques of size $k$ in $G'$, so $f(G,k)$ is a yes-instance.

*If $f(G,k)$ is a yes-instance:* $G'$ has two disjoint $k$-cliques. Since there are no edges between the original part and the added $K_k$, each clique lies entirely inside one part. At most one of them can be the added $K_k$ (they are disjoint and $K_k$ has exactly $k$ vertices), so at least one lies inside $G$ — giving $G$ a clique of size $k$.

Both directions hold, so $\text{CLIQUE} \le_p \text{DOUBLE-CLIQUE}$, and DOUBLE-CLIQUE is NP-hard. With Part 1, it is **NP-complete**.

**What the wrong direction would have shown.** A reduction DOUBLE-CLIQUE $\le_p$ CLIQUE would prove that DOUBLE-CLIQUE is *no harder than* CLIQUE. Every problem in NP satisfies that (CLIQUE is NP-complete), so it conveys no information about hardness. The asymmetry is worth restating once more: **to prove hardness, reduce from a hard problem; to prove easiness, reduce to an easy problem.**

**A consequence worked out.** Suppose someone exhibits an $O(n^5)$ algorithm for DOUBLE-CLIQUE. Then CLIQUE is solvable in polynomial time too: build $G'$ in $O(n^2)$ and call the algorithm. Since CLIQUE is NP-complete, every problem in NP reduces to CLIQUE in polynomial time, and so $P = NP$ would follow. That chain — one fast algorithm for one NP-complete problem collapses the whole class — is exactly the statement examiners test.

blocks.q: To prove that a new problem $X$ is NP-hard, one must show
blocks.exp: Hardness travels forwards along a reduction: if a known NP-hard $L$ reduces to $X$, then solving $X$ would solve $L$, so $X$ is at least as hard. Option 1 is the reverse and shows only that $X$ is no harder than $L$, which is true of every problem in NP. Option 3 is the definition of $X$ being in NP-easy territory, and option 4 is unrelated.

blocks.q: Which statement about the halting problem is correct?
opts: It is NP-hard but not NP-complete
It is in NP but not NP-hard
blocks.exp: Every problem in NP reduces to it, so it is NP-hard. But NP-completeness additionally requires membership in NP, and the halting problem is undecidable — there is no polynomial-time verifier, indeed no decider at all. NP-hard is therefore a strictly larger class than NP-complete, and it contains undecidable problems.

blocks.q: 0/1 knapsack has an $O(nW)$ dynamic programming algorithm yet is NP-complete. The correct explanation is that
opts: the algorithm is incorrect for large $W$
$W$ is exponential in the length of its binary encoding, so $O(nW)$ is not polynomial in the input size
NP-completeness only applies to decision problems, and knapsack is an optimisation problem
the algorithm uses $O(nW)$ space, and space is what matters
blocks.exp: Polynomial time means polynomial in the number of bits of input. Writing $W$ takes $\log W$ bits, so an $O(nW)$ algorithm is exponential in that measure — it is called pseudo-polynomial. Knapsack is therefore only weakly NP-complete; strongly NP-complete problems such as TSP admit no such algorithm unless P = NP.

tricks.title: Reduce FROM the hard problem
tricks.body: Write the arrow before anything else: known-hard $\le_p$ yours. Say it aloud as 'if I could solve mine, I could solve the known-hard one'. Every NP-hardness question is answered by getting this arrow the right way round.

tricks.title: NP-complete = NP-hard AND in NP
tricks.body: Two conditions, both required. A problem that is NP-hard but undecidable (halting) fails the second. Any question asking you to classify a problem is answered by testing the two conditions separately.

tricks.title: Learn the easy/hard boundary in pairs
tricks.body: 2-SAT easy, 3-SAT hard. 2-colouring easy, 3-colouring hard. Euler easy, Hamiltonian hard. Shortest path easy, longest path hard. LP easy, ILP hard. Fractional knapsack easy, 0/1 hard. Most complexity items in the exam are a single pull from this list.

tricks.title: Clique, independent set and vertex cover are the same problem
tricks.body: $S$ is a clique in $G$ iff $S$ is independent in $\bar G$ iff $V\setminus S$ is a vertex cover of $\bar G$. A question giving you one and asking for another is answered by $|VC| = V - |IS|$ and by complementing the graph.

tricks.title: Certificates are for YES instances only
tricks.body: When asked whether a problem is in NP, ask what you would show a sceptic to prove the answer is yes, and whether it can be checked quickly. If only the NO answer has a short proof, the problem is in co-NP instead.

traps.title: NP does not mean 'non-polynomial'
traps.body: It means non-deterministic polynomial. Every problem in P is also in NP. An option saying 'NP problems cannot be solved in polynomial time' is false as stated — it would be true only if $P \ne NP$ were proved, which it is not.

traps.title: NP-hard problems need not be in NP
traps.body: NP-hard only says everything in NP reduces to it. It may be undecidable, it may be an optimisation or function problem, and it may sit far above NP. Only NP-complete problems are guaranteed to be in NP.

traps.title: $P = NP$ is not known to be false
traps.body: It is unresolved. Statements such as 'since $P \ne NP$, ...' are premises, not facts. Watch for questions that ask what *would follow if* an NP-complete problem were shown to be in P — the answer is $P = NP$, not 'a contradiction'.

traps.title: A polynomial algorithm in the numeric value is not a polynomial algorithm
traps.body: $O(nW)$ knapsack, $O(nS)$ subset sum and trial-division primality are all pseudo-polynomial. Calling any of them polynomial-time, or concluding from them that the problem is in P, is the standard trap in this topic.

topics.title: Selected and Advanced Algorithms
topics.summary: String matching with KMP and Rabin-Karp, amortized analysis, randomized algorithms, number-theoretic algorithms, tries and computational geometry.

blocks.text:
## String matching

Find every occurrence of a pattern $P$ of length $m$ in a text $T$ of length $n$.

**Naive matching** tries every alignment: $\Theta((n-m+1)m)$, i.e. $\Theta(nm)$ worst case, on input like $T = a^n$, $P = a^m$. It uses no preprocessing and $O(1)$ space.

**Rabin–Karp** hashes. Compute a rolling hash of $P$ and of each length-$m$ window of $T$; compare hashes first and only verify character by character on a hash match. The rolling hash updates in $O(1)$ per shift:

$$h_{s+1} = \big((h_s - T[s]\cdot d^{m-1})\cdot d + T[s+m]\big) \bmod q$$

Expected time $O(n + m)$, **worst case $\Theta(nm)$** when every window is a spurious hit (or when $q$ is chosen badly). Its real strength is multi-pattern search and two-dimensional matching.

**Knuth–Morris–Pratt** preprocesses the pattern into a **failure function** (prefix function) $\pi$, where $\pi[i]$ is the length of the longest proper prefix of $P[1..i]$ that is also a suffix of $P[1..i]$. On a mismatch after matching $i$ characters, instead of restarting, shift so that $\pi[i]$ characters remain matched. The text pointer **never moves backwards**, so:

$$\text{preprocessing } \Theta(m), \qquad \text{matching } \Theta(n), \qquad \text{total } \Theta(n+m)$$

and the space is $\Theta(m)$. KMP is the answer whenever a question asks for worst-case linear string matching.

**Boyer–Moore** scans the pattern right to left and uses the bad-character and good-suffix rules to skip ahead, achieving sublinear **average** time — as little as $O(n/m)$ — which makes it the fastest in practice, though its worst case is $\Theta(nm)$ without the Galil rule. It is what `grep` uses.

**Aho–Corasick** generalises KMP to many patterns at once using a trie with failure links, in $O(n + \sum m_i + z)$ for $z$ occurrences.

**Z-algorithm** computes, for each position, the length of the longest substring starting there that matches a prefix of the string, in $\Theta(n)$ — an alternative to KMP that many find easier to derive.

blocks.title: Worked example — the KMP failure function
blocks.text:
Compute $\pi$ for $P = $ `A B A B C A B A B`, indices 1 to 9.

$\pi[i]$ = length of the longest proper prefix of $P[1..i]$ that is also a suffix of $P[1..i]$.

| $i$ | $P[1..i]$ | Longest prefix = suffix | $\pi[i]$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `A` | — (proper prefixes exclude the whole string) | **0** |
| 2 | `AB` | — | **0** |
| 3 | `ABA` | `A` | **1** |
| 4 | `ABAB` | `AB` | **2** |
| 5 | `ABABC` | — (`C` ends it, no prefix ends in `C`) | **0** |
| 6 | `ABABCA` | `A` | **1** |
| 7 | `ABABCAB` | `AB` | **2** |
| 8 | `ABABCABA` | `ABA` | **3** |
| 9 | `ABABCABAB` | `ABAB` | **4** |

$$\pi = [0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]$$

**How the algorithm computes it**, which is what a question may ask you to trace. Keep $k$ = current matched prefix length, starting at 0.

- $i=2$: $P[2] = $`B` $\ne P[k{+}1] = P[1] = $`A`, and $k = 0$, so $\pi[2] = 0$.
- $i=3$: $P[3] = $`A` $= P[1]$, so $k$ becomes 1, $\pi[3] = 1$.
- $i=4$: $P[4] = $`B` $= P[2]$, so $k = 2$, $\pi[4] = 2$.
- $i=5$: $P[5] = $`C` $\ne P[3] = $`A`. Fall back: $k \leftarrow \pi[2] = 0$. Now compare $P[5]$ with $P[1] = $`A` — still no match, and $k = 0$, so $\pi[5] = 0$.
- $i=6$ to $9$: each character matches the next expected one, so $k$ climbs 1, 2, 3, 4.

**Using it to search.** Suppose $T$ contains `...ABABCABAX...` and the mismatch occurs at $T$'s `X` against $P[9] = $`B`, with 8 characters matched. Instead of shifting by 1, set $k \leftarrow \pi[8] = 3$: the last 3 matched characters `ABA` are a prefix of $P$, so the pattern slides forward by $8 - 3 = 5$ positions and comparison resumes at $P[4]$ **without re-reading any text character**. That is why KMP's matching phase is $\Theta(n)$: the text index only ever increases, and $k$ can decrease at most as many times as it increased.

## Amortised analysis

Amortised analysis bounds the **average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence** — it makes no probabilistic assumption at all, which is the difference from average-case analysis. Three methods:

**Aggregate method.** Bound the total cost of $n$ operations and divide. For a stack with `MULTIPOP`, any sequence of $n$ operations costs $O(n)$ in total because each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so the amortised cost per operation is $O(1)$ even though a single `MULTIPOP` may cost $\Theta(n)$.

**Accounting method.** Charge each operation an artificial amortised cost; the surplus is stored as credit on specific objects and pays for later expensive operations. For a **dynamic array that doubles**, charge 3 units per insertion: 1 pays for the insertion itself, and 2 are saved on the new element to pay for copying it and one older element at the next resize. The invariant is that credit never goes negative.

**Potential method.** Define $\Phi$ on the data structure's state and set $\hat c_i = c_i + \Phi_i - \Phi_{i-1}$. Then $\sum \hat c_i = \sum c_i + \Phi_n - \Phi_0$, so if $\Phi_n \ge \Phi_0$ the amortised total bounds the real total. For the doubling table, $\Phi = 2n - m$ (with $n$ items in a table of size $m$) gives $\hat c = 3$ for every insertion.

Standard results to quote:

| Structure / operation | Amortised cost |
|---|---|
| Dynamic array insertion (doubling) | $O(1)$ |
| Binary counter increment | $O(1)$ (exactly 2 bit flips amortised) |
| Union-find with rank + path compression | $O(\alpha(n))$ |
| Splay tree access | $O(\log n)$ |
| Fibonacci heap insert / decrease-key | $O(1)$; extract-min $O(\log n)$ |
| Two-stack queue dequeue | $O(1)$ |

A **crucial subtlety** on the dynamic array: growing by doubling gives $O(1)$ amortised insertion, but growing by a **fixed increment** of $k$ gives $\Theta(n)$ total copy work of $\Theta(n^2/k)$, i.e. $\Theta(n)$ amortised per insertion. Growth must be geometric. Likewise shrinking should happen only when the table falls to a **quarter** full, not a half, or an alternating insert/delete sequence forces a resize every operation — this hysteresis is asked about.

## Randomised algorithms

A **Las Vegas** algorithm is always correct and has a random *running time*; randomised quicksort is the standard example, correct always and $O(n\log n)$ expected. A **Monte Carlo** algorithm always finishes in bounded time but may be *wrong* with small probability; the Miller–Rabin primality test and Karger's minimum-cut algorithm are examples. The mnemonic: **Las Vegas gambles with time, Monte Carlo gambles with correctness.**

**Randomised quicksort** picks the pivot uniformly at random, so no *input* can force the worst case — only unlucky coin flips can, and the probability of $\Theta(n^2)$ behaviour is negligible. Its expected comparison count is $2n\ln n \approx 1.39 n\log_2 n$. The worst case is still $\Theta(n^2)$; randomisation changes which inputs are bad, not the worst case itself.

**Randomised selection (quickselect)** with a random pivot runs in $\Theta(n)$ expected time by the recurrence $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$ on average.

**Karger's min cut** repeatedly contracts a uniformly random edge until two vertices remain; it returns a minimum cut with probability $\ge 2/(V(V-1))$, so $O(V^2\log V)$ independent repetitions give high confidence. This is a rare example where a very unreliable algorithm is made reliable purely by repetition.

**Skip lists** use randomised levels to get expected $O(\log n)$ search, insert and delete with far simpler code than a balanced tree.

## Number-theoretic algorithms

**Euclid's algorithm.** $\gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b)$, terminating when $b = 0$. It runs in $O(\log \min(a,b))$ divisions; the worst case is consecutive Fibonacci numbers, and by Lamé's theorem the number of steps is at most about $4.78\log_{10}$ of the smaller number. **Extended Euclid** additionally returns $x, y$ with $ax + by = \gcd(a,b)$, which is how modular inverses are computed: $a^{-1} \bmod n$ exists iff $\gcd(a,n) = 1$.

**Modular exponentiation** by repeated squaring computes $a^b \bmod n$ in $\Theta(\log b)$ multiplications instead of $b$ — the algorithm without which RSA would be unusable.

**RSA** in one line: choose primes $p, q$; set $n = pq$ and $\phi = (p-1)(q-1)$; pick $e$ coprime to $\phi$; compute $d = e^{-1} \bmod \phi$ by extended Euclid. Encryption is $c = m^e \bmod n$ and decryption $m = c^d \bmod n$. Its security rests on factoring being hard — **not** on factoring being NP-complete, which is not known.

**Miller–Rabin** is a Monte Carlo primality test with error probability at most $4^{-k}$ after $k$ rounds. **AKS** (2002) is deterministic polynomial time, which settled that PRIMES $\in$ P.

## Tries and computational geometry

A **trie** stores strings by their characters along root-to-node paths. Search, insert and delete cost $O(L)$ for a string of length $L$, **independent of how many strings are stored** — the key advantage over a hash table (no collisions, and prefix queries are natural) and over a BST ($O(L\log n)$). The cost is space: a node per character position per distinct prefix. A **compressed trie** (radix tree / Patricia trie) merges chains of single-child nodes. A **suffix tree** is a compressed trie of all suffixes of a string, buildable in $\Theta(n)$ by Ukkonen's algorithm, and it answers substring queries in $O(m)$.

**Convex hull.** Given $n$ points, find the smallest convex polygon containing them.

| Algorithm | Time | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Graham scan** | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | sort by polar angle, then one stack pass |
| **Jarvis march** (gift wrapping) | $\Theta(nh)$ | $h$ = hull vertices; beats Graham when $h$ is tiny |
| **Quickhull** | $\Theta(n\log n)$ average, $\Theta(n^2)$ worst | divide and conquer |
| **Chan's algorithm** | $\Theta(n\log h)$ | output-sensitive optimum |
| Divide and conquer | $\Theta(n\log n)$ | merge two hulls by tangent lines |

$\Omega(n\log n)$ is a lower bound for convex hull by reduction from sorting: given numbers $x_1\ldots x_n$, place them on the parabola as $(x_i, x_i^2)$; every point is on the hull and the hull order is the sorted order.

The **orientation test** underlies all of them: for points $p, q, r$ the sign of the cross product

$$(q_x - p_x)(r_y - p_y) - (q_y - p_y)(r_x - p_x)$$

is positive for a counter-clockwise turn, negative for clockwise and zero for collinear. It uses only multiplication and subtraction, so it is exact in integer arithmetic — the reason geometric code prefers it to computing angles.

Other standard geometric results: **closest pair of points** in $\Theta(n\log n)$ (topic 7.6); **line-segment intersection** among $n$ segments with $k$ crossings in $O((n+k)\log n)$ by a sweep line; **point in polygon** by ray casting in $O(n)$.

blocks.q: For the pattern `ABABCABAB`, the value of the KMP failure function at the last position is
blocks.exp: The failure value is the length of the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix. For `ABABCABAB` the suffix `ABAB` (last four characters) equals the prefix `ABAB`, and no longer proper prefix works because position 5 is `C`. So $\pi[9] = 4$, and the full array is $[0,0,1,2,0,1,2,3,4]$.

blocks.q: A dynamic array grows by a fixed increment of 10 slots each time it fills. The amortised cost of one insertion over $n$ insertions is
blocks.exp: With a fixed increment there are $n/10$ resizes, and the $i$-th copies about $10i$ elements, so the total copy work is $\sum_{i=1}^{n/10} 10i = \Theta(n^2)$, giving $\Theta(n)$ amortised per insertion. Only **geometric** growth (doubling, or any constant factor $> 1$) yields $O(1)$ amortised — which is precisely why every real dynamic array doubles.

blocks.q: Which pair correctly describes randomised quicksort and the Miller-Rabin primality test?
opts: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo respectively
Monte Carlo and Las Vegas respectively
blocks.exp: Randomised quicksort always returns a correctly sorted array; only its running time varies, so it is Las Vegas. Miller-Rabin always terminates quickly but can declare a composite number prime with bounded probability, so it is Monte Carlo. Las Vegas gambles with time, Monte Carlo with correctness.

tricks.title: Failure function by hand: match the growing prefix
tricks.body: Write the pattern, and for each position ask 'what is the longest string that is both a start and an end of this prefix'. Values rise by at most 1 per position and drop to a previous value on a mismatch, so a sanity check is that $\pi[i] \le \pi[i-1] + 1$ always.

tricks.title: KMP shift = matched length minus failure value
tricks.body: After matching $i$ characters and failing, the pattern moves forward by $i - \pi[i]$ and comparison restarts at pattern position $\pi[i]+1$. That single formula answers every 'how many positions does the pattern shift' question.

tricks.title: Growth must be geometric for $O(1)$ amortised
tricks.body: Doubling, tripling or any constant factor above 1 gives $O(1)$; adding a constant gives $\Theta(n)$. The same distinction separates $O(1)$ from $\Theta(n)$ in rehashing, in `std::vector`, and in Java's `ArrayList`.

tricks.title: Las Vegas gambles with time, Monte Carlo with correctness
tricks.body: Name the quantity that is random. If the output could be wrong, it is Monte Carlo; if only the clock is random, it is Las Vegas. A Las Vegas algorithm can always be converted to Monte Carlo by cutting it off after a deadline.

tricks.title: Convex hull inherits sorting's lower bound
tricks.body: Mapping $x_i \mapsto (x_i, x_i^2)$ turns sorting into hull construction, so any $o(n\log n)$ hull algorithm would break the comparison-sort bound. Output-sensitive $\Theta(n\log h)$ is allowed because $h$ can be much smaller than $n$.

traps.title: Amortised is not average-case
traps.body: Amortised analysis assumes nothing about the input distribution; it bounds the worst-case total of a sequence. Average-case analysis assumes a distribution. Union-find's $O(\alpha(n))$ and dynamic arrays' $O(1)$ are amortised worst case, not averages.

traps.title: Rabin-Karp is not worst-case linear
traps.body: Its expected time is $O(n+m)$ but its worst case is $\Theta(nm)$, when every window hashes to the pattern's value. KMP is the algorithm with a worst-case $\Theta(n+m)$ guarantee; Boyer-Moore is the fastest on typical text but is also $\Theta(nm)$ in the worst case without the Galil rule.

traps.title: Randomisation does not remove the worst case
traps.body: Randomised quicksort still has a $\Theta(n^2)$ worst case; what changes is that no adversary can *choose an input* to trigger it. 'Randomised quicksort has worst case $O(n\log n)$' is false.

traps.title: RSA does not rest on an NP-complete problem
traps.body: Its security rests on the hardness of factoring, which is in NP and in co-NP and is **not** known to be NP-complete — indeed if it were, $NP = \text{co-}NP$ would follow. Options asserting that breaking RSA is NP-complete are wrong.
